## 3. The scientific problem and why it matters

A newcomer opening this repository sees a registration package and will naturally read it as a registration
problem. That is the wrong frame. The reason `octreg` exists is that a set of cellular measurements, made in
centimetre-sized pieces of human brain, are currently *unplaced*, and every scientific claim anyone wants to
make from them requires them to be placed. This chapter is the part of the project that normally lives only in
the lead researcher's head: what the question is, what geometry the acquisition gives away for free and what it
destroys, why the destroyed part is the hard part, and what would count as having solved it.

This chapter uses the three provenance markers defined in chapter 2, Orientation and glossary — `[UNVERIFIED]`,
`[NOT RE-MEASURED]`, `[OPEN]`. Where a passage is an interpretation rather than a measurement, it says so in
plain words rather than carrying a marker.

Several numbers below correct figures that are still wrong in the project's own older prose —
`octreg/README.md`, `EXPLAINER_zh.md`, some figure captions. Each correction is called out where it occurs,
because a successor will otherwise meet the stale number somewhere else and conclude that this chapter is
wrong. The consolidated register of those corrections is chapter 12, Open questions and unverified claims.

**One convention used document-wide: the expected volume of a human hemisphere.** Taken from the MRI tissue
volumes this pipeline actually measured (`work/<SUBJ>/prep.json`, `mri.tissue_fraction` × field of view; also
written directly into `result.json → overlap_gate.V_mri_tissue_cm3`), the six subjects whose tissue mask
behaves sensibly span **386–806 cm³** — I48 386.3, I57 518.0, I62 531.5, I55 620.5, I46 802.9, I38 805.8 —
with a median of 576 cm³. The other three masks are broken and inflate absurdly (I56 2519.0 cm³, I61 1838.8,
I58 1453.4; §3.5.4). Note that even the sensible values include residual bath fluid and dura, so they are upper
bounds on brain tissue proper. **Wherever this document needs an expected-hemisphere figure it uses that
measured 386–806 cm³ band, and anchors any derived threshold on its 806 cm³ top** — which yields the document's
single volume-based reject gate, `1.5 × 806 ≈ 1 210 cm³`. The band is established and derived once, in
**chapter 4, The data, §4.3**; take the number from there rather than re-deriving it.

---

### 3.1 The question the data was collected to answer

The public dataset this project runs on is **DANDI:000026**, *"Human brain cell census for BA 44/45"*, funded by
NIMH grant `1U01MH117023` (a BICCN grant), published as Costantini et al., *A cellular resolution atlas of
Broca's area*, **Sci Adv 9, eadg3844** (12 October 2023), with code at
`github.com/neuroscales/biccn-broca-I46`.

The operative word in both titles is **census**. The goal was never a picture of a piece of cortex. It was a
count — how many neurons of which type sit where in Brodmann areas 44 and 45 — obtained at a resolution where
individual cells are resolved, and expressed in a coordinate system that means something *outside* the piece of
tissue the count was taken in.

The counts themselves come from design-based stereology on the light-sheet images — an Optical Fractionator
design, more than 600 sampling sites, coefficients of error below 2 %, run over 15 of 16 consecutive slices
(the last slice was damaged). The full stereology parameter list is in chapter 8, How this compares to the
published method. What matters here is that every one of those numbers is a *per-slice* measurement inside one
block of one hemisphere.

A count becomes a census only if you can say **where in the brain** it was taken, and it becomes comparable
across brains only if "where" means the same thing in each of them. The whole-hemisphere ex-vivo MRI is what
supplies that "where". Costantini et al. state the purpose of the corrected structural volume explicitly on
p. 9 of the paper: it is used to generate a brain surface and to *provide a reference coordinate system for
registration purposes*. The MRI is the reference frame **by construction** — not because it is the most
informative image (it is by far the least informative of the three), but because it is the only image of the
*whole* object, acquired before the object was cut up. Once tissue is cut, no later image can re-establish
whole-organ geometry from the pieces alone; the intact scan is the only surviving record of it.

The lab's PI, Xiangrui Zeng, gave the same motivation for the lab's own specimen when he handed over the
brainstem pair in the 2026-08-23 meeting:

> "It is a brainstem scanned with OCT, and we also have the MRI. I shared the MRI file of the brainstem crop
> with you. The MRI is a whole brain, we only cropped the region with a box, so that if you register OCT to
> MRI, in the future we will have Broca's area and other areas registered from OCT to MRI."

So the concrete, unglamorous request is this: **given a centimetre-scale tissue block imaged at micrometre
resolution, recover the map that puts it back inside the intact hemisphere it was cut from.** Every line of
`octreg` exists to produce one 4×4 matrix per block, plus enough evidence that the matrix is right.

---

### 3.2 What placing an OCT block inside the hemisphere actually buys

Four scientific products follow from that one matrix. Only the first is demonstrated by this project so far;
the remaining three are what the matrix is *for*. Each product below is grounded in a named artefact, but the
claim that they follow from the matrix is an interpretation of mine, not something anyone has measured.

**(a) Cellular measurements acquire whole-brain coordinates.** A cell count, a laminar thickness, a fibre
orientation measured inside a 15 mm block becomes a measurement at a *named anatomical location* in a
hemisphere — and therefore in any atlas that the hemisphere itself can be registered to, which is a solved
problem. Without the block→hemisphere map, the microscopy is a set of unplaced samples and the census is not a
census.

**(b) Cross-subject comparison becomes possible.** `participants.tsv` in DANDI:000026 lists **20 participants**
(the roster is in chapter 4, The data). For each subject exactly **one** reconstructed OCT block is published,
always `sample-BrocaAreaS01`, even though `samples.tsv` records many more blocks per subject (sub-I46 has
`BrocaAreaS01..S23` plus `MotorCortexS01..S08`; sub-I48 has `BrocaAreaS01..S48`). Each published block therefore
sits in a *different* brain. The only way to ask "is layer III thicker in subject A than in subject B" is to
place each block inside its own hemisphere first and then relate the hemispheres to each other. `[UNVERIFIED]` —
the exact number of participants with a published reconstructed OCT block; project memory says 12, of which 9
also have EPIC MRI plus labels, and those 9 are the set this project works from. The one-block-per-subject rule
and the size of `ses-OCT` (51 assets / 133.4 GB) are confirmed in chapter 4, The data, which also enumerates the
nine subjects actually downloaded.

**(c) Microstructure can be linked to MRI-visible contrast.** This is the product with the clearest experimental
payoff and it is currently **untouched**. The dandiset's `derivatives/EPIC/` carries, per subject, not only the
synthesised flip-angle FLASH volumes this project registers against, but **quantitative parameter maps**:
`sub-XX_ses-MRI_{PD,T1,T2star}_VFA.nii.gz` (naming is inconsistent between subjects; some appear as
`sub-XX_{PDmap,T1map,T2starmap}.nii.gz`). Once a block is registered, every OCT voxel — and through OCT, every
LSFM-stained cell — acquires a T1, a T2\* and a PD value. That is the raw material for answering what a T2\*
value physically *means* in terms of cells and myelin, which is a question a large MRI literature would like
answered. **None of these maps were downloaded.** The manifest
`~/autodl-tmp/oct-mri-registration/data/manifest_multisub.txt` on the compute server fetches only the `flip-N`
volumes and the label files; chapter 4, The data, lists exactly what was and was not fetched. Downloading them
is a small, well-scoped next step for a successor.

**(d) A completed chain to LSFM.** The OCT block is the geometric middle of a three-modality chain (§3.3).
Solving OCT→MRI completes one half of the path that carries a single stained cell all the way to hemisphere
coordinates. The other half — LSFM→OCT — was solved by Costantini et al. per slice in 2-D and is not this
project's problem.

What this project is **not**: it is not a segmentation method, not a cell-counting method, and not an atlas. It
is the coordinate plumbing that makes the science above expressible. Any writing that positions it as more than
that will be corrected by the first reviewer who reads the baseline paper.

---

### 3.3 The modality chain: LSFM → OCT → MRI

One human hemisphere is imaged three times at three scales, and **each imaging step destroys some of the
geometry the previous one had.** Understanding which step destroys what is the single most important structural
fact in this project, and it is not visible from the file names.

The full Costantini acquisition parameter tables — instrument models, optics, stage travel and accuracy,
vibratome settings, clearing protocol, digitiser and storage — live in **chapter 4, The data**, read from page
renders of the Costantini 2023 methods
(`/Users/yyttim/workspace/lsfm-project/tmp/pdfs/costantini/full_render/page-09.jpg`, `page-10.jpg`, and
`/Users/yyttim/workspace/lsfm-project/tmp/pdfs/costantini-method-11.png`, `costantini-method-12.png`). This
section quotes only the handful of numbers the geometric argument turns on.

#### 3.3.1 What each modality sees, at what resolution, and what geometry it keeps

| | **LSFM** (light-sheet fluorescence) | **OCT** (serial-sectioning block-face) | **MRI** (7 T ex vivo) |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it shows | individual labelled cells — NeuN, calretinin (CR), calbindin (Calb2), somatostatin (SST); blood vessels on the 561 nm channel | tissue backscatter: cortical laminar structure, axon bundles, vessels as dark tubes. **No cells** | proton density and relaxation contrast: gross GM/WM, vessels as dark spots |
| Physical resolution | 1.1 µm lateral, 3.7 µm axial (optical) | **5.6 µm axial** in tissue at assumed n = 1.4; **6 µm lateral** | 150 µm isotropic as acquired |
| Resolution as published / as used here | deskewed and downsampled to **3.3 µm isotropic**, JPEG2000 lossy 1:20 | reconstructed volumes at **12 / 20 / 30–35 µm** depending on subject | EPIC derivatives at **0.12 mm** (7 of our 9 subjects) or **0.15 mm** (I46, I55); the lab's own brainstem MRI is **0.08 mm** |
| Field of view per unit | 1.1 × 1.1 mm stacks, 100 µm overlap between contiguous stacks | 3 × 3 mm tiles, 10 % tile overlap | whole hemisphere, FOV 192 × 81.3 mm |
| Instrument (specs in chapter 4, The data) | custom inverted dual-objective light sheet, the two objectives at 90° to each other and both inclined 45° to the holder plane — which is why a deskew is needed before the slice is even flat | custom polarisation-sensitive OCT (PSOCT). **Only the intensity channel is used**, which is why the paper and this project both just say "OCT" | Siemens MAGNETOM Terra 7 T; multi-echo VFA FLASH with **bipolar readout**, flip angles 10 / 20 / 30° acquired separately — the bipolar readout is the reason the EPIC correction exists |
| Geometry it **preserves** | within a single slice, after the 45° deskew | **the entire 3-D block**, because the block never moves | **the entire intact hemisphere**, because nothing was cut |
| Geometry it **destroys** | everything *between* slices: the slice is physically removed, transported, cleared, swollen, folded, compressed | nothing geometric — but it destroys the specimen: after imaging, the block is a stack of 500 µm slices | nothing — but it resolves nothing below ≈0.1 mm, so it cannot see laminae, axon bundles or anything cellular |

A note on why the MRI needed so much correction machinery, because it changes what "the MRI" is: bipolar
readout gradients distort odd and even echoes in *opposite* directions under B0 inhomogeneity, so the echoes
misalign. The authors correct this with a group-sparsity, edge-preserving joint intensity-correction algorithm
that uses a B0 field map plus all the FLASH images together; there is no body coil on that 7 T scanner, so
receive-bias correction is model-based rather than acquisition-based, using a likelihood cost that jointly
segments tissue type and estimates the bias. The DANDI derivatives directory is literally named `EPIC` after
that method (Varadarajan et al., "Edge-preserving B0 inhomogeneity distortion correction for high-resolution
multi-echo ex vivo MRI at 7 T"). **The volume `octreg` registers against is therefore already a derived,
corrected, synthesised FLASH contrast, not raw scanner output** — which matters when reasoning about residual
intensity bias (§3.4.2). Chapter 4, The data, has the full description of the EPIC derivative and what it was
built from.

#### 3.3.2 Why OCT is the geometric bridge

**The OCT block never leaves the stage.** After clearing, the block is embedded in agarose and mounted on
motorised xyz stages whose **unidirectional moving accuracy is 2 / 2 / 10 µm**. The exposed top surface is
raster-scanned as 3 × 3 mm tiles; a vibratome then shaves **500 µm** off the top **in place**; and the newly
exposed surface is scanned with the stage coordinates still valid. A single LabVIEW program drives both the
imaging and the slicing. (Stage and vibratome models, clearing chemistry and timings: chapter 4, The data.)

Reconstruction, per p. 10 of the paper: tiles are stitched in 2-D using average-intensity projection, linearly
blended in x and y once each tile's coordinate is known, **"and then stacked in z"**. There is *no* image-based
inter-slab registration along z. The z stacking is a bookkeeping operation using the stage's 10 µm coordinates —
which is at or below one depth voxel for every subject in this project.

Two consequences follow, and a newcomer must hold both at once:

- **Good:** the reconstructed OCT volume is **one rigid 3-D object** with a real, if imperfect, internal
  coordinate system. It can be related to the MRI by a single *global* affine. That is not an assumption — this
  project measured it. A free-form deformation stage was implemented, run on I46 and **not shipped**, because
  the measured gain is at the level of noise; the full ablation is in chapter 6, What we found, and what it
  means. Costantini et al. reached the same conclusion independently — they have an SVF stage
  (`mri2oct_nonlin.sh`) and the paper says it is unnecessary for MRI↔OCT.
- **Bad:** because z is bookkeeping rather than measurement, **any error in the assumed z step is a global scale
  error along the depth axis, and nothing in the image contradicts it.** This is exactly the failure mode that
  bit subject I46 (§3.4.4) and it is the reason the vascular stage exists.

#### 3.3.3 Why LSFM is not the bridge

**The LSFM slices are the shavings, and they lose their geometry in transit.** The 500 µm slices the vibratome
removes are what goes to the light sheet. Per p. 10, each slice is *manually captured to preserve the
sequence*, packed, labelled, stacked and **shipped to another site**, where it is cleared, antigen-retrieved,
stained over several days and finally squeezed between a coverslip and a spacer. By the time the light sheet
sees it, the slice has been detached, transported, swollen, shrunk, folded and compressed. **Whatever pose it
had relative to the block is gone.** (The step-by-step protocol is in chapter 4, The data.)

Therefore **OCT is the geometric reference for LSFM, and not the other way round.** The OCT block still
contains, in its correct place, the exact 500 µm slab each LSFM slice came from. Costantini et al. exploit this
literally, and their own code is the proof:

| Their script | What it does | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| `scripts/registration/oct2lsfm_affine.sh` | loops `for i in {08..23}`, registering each LSFM slice to `oct/slices/unstack/oct.${i}.masked.nii.gz` — the *unstacked* corresponding OCT slab — with `@affine affine -2d` | the affine is forced 2-D; there is no inter-slice 3-D pose estimation anywhere |
| `oct2lsfm_nonlin.sh` | `@nonlin svf 1 -2d ...` | the deformation is also 2-D, per slice |
| `lsfm_slide_center_and_scale.py` | resizes each slide crop to exactly 50 z-samples, sets the z voxel size to `0.396 / 50` mm = **7.92 µm**, and re-centres the affine on `centeroct`, the centre of `oct/slices/unstack/oct.{i}.nii.gz` | the LSFM slice's z geometry is **imported from OCT**, not measured |
| `lsfm2oct_make_lsfm_volume.py` | pulls every slice through its own `oct2lsfm` transform into a common OCT-derived grid at `[0.0099, 0.0099, 0.00792]` mm | it is a warp-and-accumulate into OCT space, **not a reconstruction** |

```
  cells                         geometry                          anatomy
  -----                         --------                          -------
  LSFM slice i  --2D affine + 2D SVF, per slice, vessel-guided-->  OCT slab i
                                                              |
                                     OCT block (one rigid 3-D object)
                                                              |
                                         --3D affine (+optional SVF)-->  whole-hemisphere MRI
                                                                                  ^
                                                                        this arrow is octreg v1
```

Reconstructing LSFM *across* slices without an OCT block-face reference — recovering slice order, orientation
and inter-slice deformation — is a separate and unsolved problem. That is the lab's older project (§3.6).
`octreg v1` deliberately does not touch it, and a newcomer should **not** assume the OCT block has to pass
through any reconstruction pipeline. OCT is already a volume.

#### 3.3.4 The two specimens this project actually holds

| | **DANDI:000026 subset** | **Xiangrui Zeng's own pair** |
|---|---|---|
| Path (AutoDL) | `~/autodl-tmp/oct-mri-registration/data/costantini/dandi-000026/` | `~/autodl-tmp/oct-mri-registration/data/xiangrui/OCT_to_MRI/` |
| Origin | public, downloaded via `download_costantini.sh` (16-asset sub-I46 subset) and `manifest_multisub.txt` | `/shared/u/xiangruz/registration/OCT_to_MRI/` on xulab, created 2026-08-13, unchanged since |
| Size / files | 64,730,457,001 B (60.28 GiB), 97 files, **9 subjects** | 13,117,697,928 B (12.22 GiB), **2 files** |
| Anatomy | Broca's area cortex, `sample-BrocaAreaS01` for every subject | human **brainstem**, donor I58 |
| OCT | 12–35 µm, OME-TIFF / ImageJ TIFF; block extents from 7.5 × 15.3 × 14.8 mm (I46) to 26.9 × 37.5 × 60.6 mm (I57) | `I58_Brainstem_mus_Slice_full_20um_corr.nii.gz`, 13,025,490,607 B, 20 µm isotropic NIfTI, `(1457, 2013, 1595)` = 29.14 × 40.26 × 31.90 mm |
| MRI | EPIC-corrected VFA FLASH at 0.12 or 0.15 mm, **whole hemisphere** | `I58_brainstem_MRI_cropped_to_OCT.nii.gz`, 92,207,321 B, 0.08 mm, `(343, 489, 495)` = 27.44 × 39.12 × 39.60 mm, **already box-cropped to the block** |

No labels, no segmentations, no vessel annotations, no landmarks, no reference transform of any kind** — verified by directly listing `/shared/u/xiangruz/registration/OCT_to_MRI/` on xulab, which contains those two files and nothing else |

Two traps a successor will hit:

1. **The donor-I58 name collision is real.** DANDI `sub-I58` is a **Broca's area** cortical block at
   30/30/35 µm; Xiangrui's I58 is a **brainstem** block at 20 µm. Same donor, different specimen, unrelated
   results (`work/runs/I58_otsu` versus `work/runs/xiangrui_I58bs` / `xiangrui_I58bs_novasc`). Never merge them.
2. **The promised additional subjects do not exist yet.** `/shared/u/xiangruz/registration/` on xulab contains
   only `OCT_to_MRI` and nothing else; the 20+ subjects that were mentioned have not been uploaded (directory
   listing of 2026-08-23; chapter 10, State of play: where everything is, has the current listing).

### 3.4 Why this registration is hard

Eight difficulties. Several standard registration assumptions fail *simultaneously* here, which is why
off-the-shelf tools do not simply work and why the pipeline looks as unusual as it does. Each one is stated with
the number that makes it concrete.

#### 3.4.1 Partial-to-whole, at a scale ratio that varies forty-fold

The moving image is a small fraction of the fixed image, and it is not centred, not oriented and not bounded.
Same-subject ratios, computed from `prep.json` block extents against the pipeline's own MRI tissue-mask volume:

| subject | OCT block bounding box | MRI tissue volume (own subject) | block / hemisphere |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| I38 | 29.12 × 51.72 × 47.19 mm = **71.07 cm³** | 805.8 cm³ | **8.8 %** |
| I62 | 21.00 × 36.93 × 45.00 mm = **34.90 cm³** | 531.5 cm³ | **6.6 %** |
| I46 | 7.52 × 15.25 × 14.76 mm = **1.69 cm³** | 802.9 cm³ | **0.21 %** |

Each hemisphere figure is that subject's own measured MRI tissue volume, not a stand-in; against the 806 cm³
top of the document's measured band (chapter 4, The data, §4.3) the three ratios are 8.8 %, 4.3 % and 0.21 %.
Either way the search target ranges
over roughly a factor of forty in relative size — from a 15 mm cortical cube that is two parts in a thousand of
the hemisphere, up to a 50 mm slab that is nearly a tenth of it. Two design consequences follow directly:

- **A similarity that integrates over the fixed image is meaningless.** Every metric in `octreg` is masked to
  the block: mean and variance are computed only inside the template mask, so the hemisphere's statistics
  outside the block never enter the score.
- **The overlap requirement had to become adaptive.** The naive requirement `--min-overlap 0.85` is
  unsatisfiable when the OCT mask includes embedding medium (§3.4.6), so `register.py:111` lowers the gate to a
  fraction of the achievable maximum, with a hard floor so it can never vanish. The formula, the floor and the
  observed per-run values are stated once, in full, in chapter 5, The method, as a chain of reasoning; several
  older prose documents quote it without the floor, which is the version to distrust.

The inverse case also exists, and it is the lab's own data. On the brainstem pair the **MRI is already cropped
to the block**, while the OCT "tissue" mask (28.9 cm³, agarose included) is more than twice the MRI's tissue
volume (13.3 cm³), so the effective overlap the gate could demand was **0.369**, not the requested 0.85.

**Correction to how the adaptive gate is usually described:** the gate **never binds on any DANDI subject**. In
all eight DANDI runs that record it, `result.json → overlap_gate` is `{requested 0.85, effective 0.850}`. It
binds *only* on the brainstem pair (0.369). And `work/runs/I46_otsu/result.json` has `overlap_gate: null` — the
gate did not exist when I46 was run. Describing it as a live feature of the DANDI results is wrong; it is a
feature that exists *because of* the lab's own data.

#### 3.4.2 Cross-modality with no shared intensity relationship

OCT intensity is optical backscatter. MRI intensity is a synthesised FLASH contrast built from relaxation
parameters. There is no monotone mapping between them, and no reliable non-monotone one either. This was
measured, not assumed:

- **Raw-intensity NCC between the 20 µm OCT and the 0.08 mm MRI on the brainstem pair: 0.033** at a 0.32 mm
  pyramid level and **0.030** at 0.16 mm (`octreg/scripts/test_polish.py`, `logs/test_polish.log`).
- Worse than useless in practice: running that intensity-based polish stage from a pose a human had judged
  correct **moved the block 9.37 mm in centre, 15.79° in rotation, and 9.55 mm corner-mean away from it.** An
  intensity term does not merely fail to help here; it actively destroys a good solution.

That measurement is the whole justification for the pipeline's central representational choice: **both sides are
reduced to a two-class WM/GM map before anything is correlated.** The class map is the only representation in
which these two modalities are comparable at all. Everything downstream — the masked NCC, the FFT search, the
polarity ambiguity — is a consequence of that choice.

The enabling preprocessing step on the MRI side is **bias-field flattening**: divide by the local mean at
σ = 10 mm before thresholding. On I46 it takes the MRI feature map from **0.66 / 0.62** to **0.90 / 0.93** Dice
(WM / GM) against the dataset's own manual labels — a step change, not a tweak. The improvement has been
re-derived and is confirmed; quote it freely. The precise pair, given here once:

| MRI feature construction | Dice WM vs manual labels | Dice GM vs manual labels |
|---|---:|---:|
| plain Otsu on raw EPIC intensity | **0.6502** | **0.5987** |
| Otsu after local-mean flattening (σ = 10 mm) | **0.9069** | **0.9343** |

The reason it works is that the hemisphere carries a **1.9× intensity drift** (local-mean field p5 29.3, p50
36.6, p95 55.4) — residual receive-coil bias that survived the EPIC correction, unsurprising given there is no
body coil on that scanner. A global Otsu threshold cannot survive a 1.9× multiplicative field; a local one can.
Without that single division, a label-free whole-hemisphere Otsu split is not viable, and the entire label-free
premise of the project collapses. This is the highest-leverage line of preprocessing in the codebase.

#### 3.4.3 Unknown pose, including handedness — and a fourth unknown nobody expects

The block's orientation relative to the hemisphere is not recorded anywhere in the data. Neither is its
**chirality** — whether the reconstruction is mirrored — because a serial-sectioning stack's z direction and its
in-plane axis convention are set by acquisition software and file-writing conventions, not by anatomy.

This is not hypothetical, and it is not a property of sloppy data: **within the same dataset, processed by the
same group, 6 of 9 subjects register mirrored and 3 do not.**

| mirrored (`final_transform.mirror = true`) | not mirrored |
|---|---|
| **I38, I46, I48, I56, I58, I62** | **I55, I57, I61**, and both brainstem runs |

**Correction:** `EXPLAINER_zh.md:13` and several older result write-ups say "5 of 9" and list I46, I38, I56,
I58, I62. The verified count is **6 of 9**; **I48 is the one that was dropped** — read from
`final_transform.mirror` in all nine `work/runs/I*_otsu/result.json` and confirmed by the `mirror` column of
`work/runs/summary_all/summary.md`.

So the coarse search space is 8000 quasi-uniform SO(3) rotations × {identity, mirror} = **16,000 orientations**,
with all translations evaluated at once per orientation by FFT, at 0.6 mm. What that costs, stated honestly —
this is one of the most frequently mis-quoted numbers in the whole project:

> An exhaustive 16,000-orientation search over all translations costs **45 s** on a 0.08 mm brainstem crop and
> **298.9 s** on a 0.15 mm whole hemisphere with the label-free Otsu features (**153.7 s** with the
> parser-probability features); the shipped wrapper runs it **once per class polarity**, so budget **597.8 s** of
> search for a whole hemisphere. Across the corpus, single-branch search ranges **44.8 s – 1010.3 s**.

**Why the widely-quoted "150 s" / "154 s" is misleading:** 153–154 s *is* a real, logged, full
16,000-orientation whole-hemisphere search time (`logs/run_whole_final.log` "search done in 153s",
`logs/run_whole_final2.log` "154s"), but it comes from
`octreg/scripts/run_demo_i46.py` whose `--features` default is **`mixed`** — *MRI parser probabilities* plus
OCT intensity-derived WM/GM. That is **not the training-free path**. `register.py` accepts only
`choices=["otsu","parser"]`; `mixed` does not exist there and `octreg/features.py::build_features` raises
`ValueError` on it. Quoting 154 s under "we removed the labels" attributes a parser-assisted runtime to the
label-free pipeline. It also happens that the 8000/16000 halfway progress tick of `reg_I46_otsu.log` is 150 s,
which is what made the confusion so durable.

Related correction: `--oct-wm-bright auto` is **not** `register.py`'s default —
`register.py:32` declares `choices=["auto","yes","no"], default="no"`. Every DANDI run passed it explicitly
because `run_subject.sh` line 21 hard-codes it. The 2× doubling is a property of the shipped wrapper, and a
successor invoking `register.py` directly will silently get single-polarity behaviour and a different answer.

**Class polarity is the fourth unknown, and it is worse than the other three.** Which of the two Otsu classes is
white matter also flips between subjects — **I46 is GM-bright, I55 is WM-bright** — and, critically, **the
coarse search prefers the wrong answer**:

| I46, polarity branch | coarse search top-1 (0.6 mm) | refined NCC |
|---|---:|---:|
| losing (wrong) branch | **0.7411** | 0.7300 |
| winning (correct) branch | 0.7259 | **0.7564** |

Only the *refined* NCC separates them. Chapter 5, The method, as a chain of reasoning, carries the full
polarity-symmetry argument and the deliberately-wrong run that demonstrates it. A method that trusted its own coarse score — which is what most
template-matching pipelines do — would confidently place I46 at the wrong pose with the wrong polarity, and
would report a high score while doing it. This is the concrete reason the pipeline refines the top-k coarse
candidates rather than committing to the argmax.

#### 3.4.4 Unknown scale along exactly one axis, and an objective that cannot see it

The depth (serial-sectioning) axis is the axis whose spacing is bookkeeping rather than measurement (§3.3.2). It
is also the axis the tissue's own geometry cannot constrain, and that was measured directly:
`octreg/scripts/scale_probe.py` stretches the I46 block along one array axis at a time, from 0.85× to 1.30×,
and records what the objective does.

**The result, in one line: along the two in-plane axes the objective has a sharp peak, and along the depth axis
it is a flat plateau — the NCC moves by 0.021 over the whole depth sweep against 0.169 along the in-plane k
axis, a factor of eight, and the manual-label Dice moves by 0.007.** The three-axis table with every number,
plus the correction to an earlier write-up that read only the ascending half of the depth curve and so
understated the flatness, is in chapter 6, What we found, and what it means. A two-class cortical sheet does not
encode its own thickness scale, **and neither do the manual GM/WM labels**.

The practical warning this yields is general, not specific to this dataset: **anyone doing OCT→MRI with a
structure-only similarity will silently absorb a large error along one axis and never see it in the objective.**
That is a negative result that stands on its own and is arguably the most transferable thing this project has
produced.

The fix, and its corroboration, both come from vasculature — vessels are the only structure that is
simultaneously visible in both modalities (dark tubes in OCT backscatter, dark spots in ex-vivo FLASH) and that
carries a length scale:

| Estimate of I46's depth-axis scale | Value | Provenance |
|---|---:|---|
| sibling subjects' OCT metadata (35/30 = 14/12) | **1.1667** | every other subject's sidecar |
| Costantini et al.'s published affine, largest column norm | **1.17419** | `results/mri2oct/affine.lta`, fitted *with* a hand-drawn-vessel term |
| oracle affine fitted in our frame to manual labels + manual vessels | **1.177** | `octreg/results/final/summary/refine_validate.json`, row `B1: ORACLE affine (manual)` |
| structural stage only, no vessel channel | **1.026** (`I46_otsu`) / **1.032** (`crop_*` experiments) | it does not see the stretch at all |
| our fully automatic vessel channel, shipped default `--vascular-w 2.0` | **1.219** (`I46_otsu` final) / **1.223** (standalone `vessel_channel_refine.json`) | `work/runs/I46_otsu/result.json → final_transform.stretch_ijk[0]` |
| same, weight sweep 0.5 → vessel-only | 1.144 → 1.237 | `vessel_channel_refine.json` |
| auto, MRI Frangi × OCT DANDI `ves_seg` | 1.183 | ibid. |

Three independent routes agree at **1.167 / 1.174 / 1.177**, and an automatic channel that saw none of them
lands at **1.14–1.24**. That is agreement at the **±0.05 level on a quantity the structural objective cannot
measure**. It is **not** agreement to three decimals and must never be written up as such (§3.7 item 3).

`[UNVERIFIED]` — some older project prose says "the true scale is about **1.18**". No artefact on disk carries
1.18. The two defensible anchors are the pipeline's own **1.219** and the sidecar-vs-siblings ratio
**14/12 = 1.1667**. Whoever writes this up must pick one and say which.

**A caveat that must travel with this story.** The end-to-end result supports it — enabling the vascular stage
moves I46's depth stretch **1.026 → 1.219** and the honest vessel metric from **265 µm → 167 µm** — but the
single-axis probe does *not* corroborate it cleanly. In `scale_profiles.json` the vessel metric responds
strongly on the **k** axis (f150 0.254 → 0.317 at s = 1.10) and stays flat at 0.23–0.26 along **i / depth**. A
single-axis probe about the block centre and a full 12-DOF affine are different experiments, so this is
plausibly axis coupling, but it is **unresolved and marked [UNVERIFIED]**. Anyone re-deriving it should re-run
`scale_probe.py` from the *final* transform and report the i-axis profile of the **vessel-channel NCC**, not the
mixed NCC.

**The reverse control is I55**, the other 12 µm in-plane block, whose sidecar *does* record the anisotropic
spacing (14/12/12 µm). Its depth stretch is **0.913** — i.e. no correction needed — and the vascular stage moves
the block by only **0.334 mm**. A method that "found" a large depth correction on I55 would be finding an
artefact of its own optimiser.

**But I55 is not a clean null, and the caveat must travel with it.** Read the *anisotropy* rather than the
depth stretch alone. I55's structural solution is `stretch_ijk = [0.92, 1.084, 1.063]`, so the recovered
depth-to-in-plane ratio is 0.92 / 1.0735 = **0.8570** — which is 6/7 = 0.8571, to within two parts in ten
thousand, and 6/7 is **exactly the inverse of the 7/6 = 1.1667 factor that I46's sidecar is accused of
missing**. The two subjects therefore land on reciprocal values of the same suspicious ratio. That may be
coincidence: 12 µm in-plane blocks with a 14 µm depth step are the same acquisition family, and an optimiser
free to trade depth against in-plane scale has no reason to avoid 6/7. But nobody has shown it *is* coincidence,
and until someone does, I55 cannot be presented as an unqualified independent null — a shared systematic that
produced 7/6 on I46 could produce 6/7 here. `[OPEN]`. The cheap check is to run the same anisotropy readout on
the seven 30/30/35 µm subjects, which are a different acquisition family, and see whether 6/7 and 7/6 keep
appearing.

**Correction:** `octreg/README.md:42` and several older gotcha tables say I55 needs "only a 1.10 depth stretch".
The verified value is **0.913**; the final `stretch_ijk = [0.913, 1.097, 1.084]` and index 0 is depth — 1.097 is
the in-plane **j** axis. This is the `stretch_ijk` / `column_scales` index confusion described in chapter 6,
What we found, and what it means. The *argument* survives; the number does not.

#### 3.4.5 Unreliable metadata

Every one of the following was found by reading files against pixels, not by being told:

| Defect | Detail |
|---|---|
| **The I46 depth spacing is simply wrong** | The sidecar `sub-I46_ses-OCT_sample-BrocaAreaS01_OCT.json` says `"PixelSize": [12, 12, 12]` µm. Every sibling says 30/30/35 or 12/12/14 — ratio 7/6 = 1.1667. I46's OME-XML carries the placeholder `PhysicalSize = 1.0 "pixel"` and `XResolution = 0`, so **nothing inside the file contradicts the sidecar**. A fix flag exists (`prep_subject.py --oct-spacing-um 14,12,12`) and **was never used**: every stored `work/I46/*` array is built on 12 µm depth |
| **`flip-N` is an index, not an angle** | For sub-I58, `flip-1` is **FlipAngle 30**, `flip-3` is **FlipAngle 10** (both TR 0.045, Siemens MAGNETOM Terra 7 T, GRE). I58 was registered against `flip-3`, i.e. the **10°** volume, which has almost no GM/WM contrast — that is why it failed. The 30° volume `sub-I58_ses-MRI_flip-1_VFA.nii.gz` (**2,890,933,645 B**) is on disk and was never tried. Seven of nine subjects are 20° regardless of index; I48's angle is unknown because its sidecar was never downloaded. Some older project prose has this **inverted** — always read the sidecar, never the index (chapter 4, The data) |
| **Units bug in a sidecar** | I55's `RepetitionTime` is the string `"34"` where every other subject has `0.034` |
| **Vessel-label values are not standardised** | `1` (I38/I58/I61/I62), `255` (I46/I48/I56/I57), `30` (I55), plus 17 voxels of `−32768` in I57 — an int16 sentinel written into an int32 file. Always threshold `> 0` |
| **Label volumes are on their own grids and axis orders** | `seg-wholehemi` is always stored R,A,S and therefore always permuted relative to the EPIC MRI; five label files are bounding-box crops, not full-FOV volumes |
| **The label→MRI axis pairing is broken for the six 0.12 mm subjects** | `prep_subject.py::map_labels_to_grid` derives `perm = [1,2,0]` from the affines for **I38, I48, I56, I57, I58, I61**, pairing a 640-voxel label axis against a 1400-voxel MRI axis. Only **36–40 %** of the MRI grid is reachable and **31.7–41.6 %** of the whole-hemisphere labels are dropped. The shape-consistent pairing `transpose(1,2,0)` retains all 3,856,521 I38 labels and puts **99.0 %** of them on tissue versus 87.8 % now. `[UNVERIFIED]` — measured once and unchallenged, but not re-derived |
| **OCT vessel segmentations are not on the OCT grid** | I46's `ves_seg.tif` has **561** z-slices against the OCT's **627**; I38 and I48 differ on all three axes. The code does `full[:nz] = seg[:nz]`, defensible only for I46, and even there the 0-vs-66 slice offset could not be resolved statistically |
| **The authors' own published affine cannot be recovered into our frame** | The OCT side has **no world coordinates at all**. Scanning 96 signed axis permutations, the best conventions (`SRP` 95.8 %, `SPR` 94.8 %, `IRP` 93.8 % of OCT tissue inside the BA labels) place the block correctly at millimetre scale, but MRI-vessel-to-`ves_seg` median distance is **≥ 260 µm for every convention** against a ±3 mm random-shift control whose *best* is 346 µm. The authors' coarse placement and ours differ by **23 mm** on I46 and this is unresolved |
| **I62 has no whole-hemisphere label at all** | and DANDI additionally carries a mis-named `derivatives/Labels/ses-I61/` directory containing a JSON and no NIfTI |

The operational lesson, and it should be written on the wall: **treat every header, sidecar and label file as a
hypothesis to be checked against the pixels.** The one metadata bug that actually changed a scientific
conclusion — I46's depth spacing — survived precisely because there was no second record to check it against.

#### 3.4.6 Tissue deformation and sectioning artefacts

The block is not the shape it was inside the head, and the images carry structured artefacts that look like
anatomy to generic feature detectors.

- **The slab sawtooth.** Each 500 µm cut has its own depth-attenuation profile, so the reconstructed volume
  carries a periodic intensity modulation along z. Measured directly by FFT and autocorrelation of the
  per-slice in-tissue median: period **33 slices for I46 (0.396 mm)** and **12 slices for I56 (0.420 mm)**, with
  clean harmonics. `[NOT RE-MEASURED]` — the measurement stands, but re-running `/tmp/period.py` on the compute
  server would settle it. Any raw-intensity similarity, LCC included, is corrupted by this, and removing it is
  exactly what the per-slice median normalisation in `prep_subject.py` is for.

  **Correction, and it matters for a reader who checks the code:** `prep_subject.py:125` carries the comment
  `# ~1.2 mm of depth = one section period at 12 um`, and some older project prose puts the period at "≈100
  slices". Both are wrong by about 3×. The "≈100" originates in
  `/Users/yyttim/workspace/lsfm-project/costantini_b0/reports/costantini_i46_data_audit.md:43`, where a mean
  profile was inspected at **25-slice granularity** — which aliases a true 33-slice period to ≈100.

  **What this measurement does *not* do is confirm the I46 depth-spacing bug, and an earlier version of this
  chapter claimed that it did. That claim is withdrawn.** The tempting argument was: 500 µm of cut divided by a
  33-slice period gives 15.15 µm per slice, therefore the sidecar's 12 µm is too small. It fails on its own
  sibling. Apply it to **I56**, whose 35 µm sidecar is corroborated twice over, and a 12-slice period gives
  500/12 = **41.7 µm** — a 19 % error against a spacing nobody disputes. Read consistently, i.e. correcting I46
  by the same 1.19 factor by which the argument overshoots on I56, it implies a depth correction of only about
  **1.06**, not the 1.167 the sidecar-vs-siblings ratio gives. So the section-period measurement is real and
  worth keeping as a description of the artefact, but it is **not** an independent line of evidence about I46's
  spacing, and it must not be cited as one. The depth-spacing case rests on the three converging estimates in
  §3.4.4 (sibling metadata, the authors' published affine, the oracle affine), and on nothing else.

- **Frangi fires on the artefacts, not the vessels, at the wrong scale.** On the raw 12 µm I46 stack, Frangi
  picks up speckle and nothing else — which is why the OCT vessel channel is computed at a physical scale
  (`sigmas_vox = (1.0, 1.5, 2.2)`, ≈24–35 µm) after pooling, not on raw voxels. On the brainstem pair it picks
  up the **section seams**: **4,534,410 "vessel" voxels** that are a map of the sectioning grid, giving a
  vessel-channel NCC of **0.0055** and **0/8** vascular restarts within 0.3 mm. The vascular stage is switched
  off for that pair — and it had consumed **4,778 s of the run's 5,244 s** of wall clock to make the result
  worse. (`xiangrui_I58bs_novasc`, the same pair without it, finishes in **362.3 s**.)

- **The embedding medium is not separable by intensity.** Agarose scatters like tissue: at `raw tissue thr 0.0`,
  **77.9 %** of the brainstem block classifies as tissue. That is why the OCT mask is 28.9 cm³ against the MRI's
  13.3 cm³, and it is the root cause of the adaptive overlap gate (§3.4.1).

- **Non-rigid deformation is small for this modality pair.** Measured, not assumed: the oracle non-rigid
  displacement field is a fraction of a millimetre and the Dice gain is at the level of noise, which is why the
  stage was built and then left out of v1. The ablation numbers are in chapter 6, What we found, and what it
  means. Both this project and Costantini et al. conclude that an affine suffices for MRI↔OCT. **The deformation
  problem lives on the LSFM side of the chain**, which is the other project (§3.6).

#### 3.4.7 Near-total absence of labels

This is a constraint on the *method*, not merely on the evaluation, and it is the single design driver a
newcomer is most likely to misread as an aesthetic preference. The PI, 2026-08-23:

> "We do have a lot of scans and volumes, but we do not have many labels."

Concretely:

| Where | What labels exist |
|---|---|
| The lab's own brainstem specimen | **two files and nothing else** — no labels, no masks, no landmarks, no transform (verified by direct listing) |
| DANDI:000026, OCT vessel segmentations | **5 of 20 participants**: I38, I45, I46, I48, I60. We hold three (I38, I46, I48), and **two of those three are on a grid that does not match their own OCT** |
| DANDI:000026, MRI labels | drawn by hand on **every 10th slice**, interpolated with SmartInterpol, then touched up by hand |

Now compare the baseline this project is measured against. Costantini et al.'s `mri2oct_affine.sh` requires
hand-drawn GM, hand-drawn WM and hand-drawn vessels **on both modalities** — six annotation products — plus an
MRI pre-cropped to the block's known location. Their similarity is
`lcc --patch 5%` (w 1) + `dice` GM (w 0.5) + `dice` WM (w 0.5) + `ndot` vessel MED (w 0.1); four of those five
terms need annotation. **That recipe cannot be run on data that has none of them.** The label-free design of
`octreg v1` is a response to a stated operational constraint of this lab, not a methodological preference, and
that is how it should be defended in a lab meeting.

#### 3.4.8 One difficulty that turned out to be optional

For honesty, and because it changes how the work should be positioned: **the whole-hemisphere blind search is
not operationally required.** From the same 2026-08-23 meeting:

> **Yuntian:** "So we do not need to do a global search over the whole hemisphere of the MRI?"
> **Xiangrui:** "We do not. We know where it is, so we can crop a small part there. And the I58 data I shared
> with you is already cropped."

The cropped path already exists in the code (`register.py --crop-centre x,y,z --crop-half-mm 30`), and on I46
the cropped and prior-free paths converge to the same solution. So the global search is **robustness insurance
and a paper capability, not the value proposition.** The *label-free* half of the claim is entirely untouched by
this — that constraint is real and stated by the PI himself (§3.4.7).

`[OPEN]` — what the prior actually *is* has never been specified: a region label, a cutting record, a coordinate
range, a manual ROI. Nobody has said. This must be asked before any prior-conditioned search radius is designed,
and until it is answered, no outward-facing text should describe the prior as a precise ROI or set of
coordinates.

---

### 3.5 What "success" would mean, and why Dice is a weak criterion here

#### 3.5.1 The definition

Success is: **the recovered transform places the block where the tissue actually came from, to a residual small
enough that a measurement made inside the block can be attributed to the right anatomy.** For cortex, "right
anatomy" means the right gyrus and the right cortical depth, so the residual has to be comfortably under the
≈2.5 mm cortical thickness. **Nothing in this project has yet measured a residual in those terms on real data.**

There are two regimes and the PI drew the line between them explicitly:

> "during development I usually prefer to just check visually whether things look right... Although for a paper
> we need some quantitative results."

So: **visual QC and consistency checks drive the development loop; a defensible quantitative protocol is still
owed for the paper.** These are different bars. Conflating them in writing is the most likely way this project
gets embarrassed.

#### 3.5.2 Why Dice against manual labels is a weak criterion

The headline number the project has reported is Dice ≈ **0.803 / 0.825** (I46, WM/GM) and ≈ **0.921 / 0.930**
(I55) of the registered OCT class map against the dataset's own manual GM/WM labels. Six independent reasons
why that number should not be the target:

1. **A wrong pose can score better — the single most important fact in this chapter.** The deliberately-wrong
   run `I46_parser_wrongpol_v0` places the block about **70 mm** from the correct centre and still scores a
   *higher* WM Dice than the correct run, and a higher coarse search score too. What separates them is evidence
   Dice does not use: the vessel channel and the vascular restart consistency, both of which collapse for the
   wrong pose. The side-by-side table is in chapter 5, The method, as a chain of reasoning. The reason is
   structural, not accidental: **a hemisphere is mostly a two-class folded sheet, so a plausible-but-wrong
   cortical location reproduces the same local statistics Dice measures.**
2. **The labels themselves are geometrically corrupted for two-thirds of the subjects.** The axis-pairing defect
   (§3.4.5) means every Dice computed for **I38, I48, I56, I57, I58, I61** is against a label volume that lost
   31.7–41.6 % of its content and can only be sampled over 36–40 % of the MRI grid.
3. **The labels are annotation, and carry annotation error.** Drawn on every 10th slice, SmartInterpol-
   interpolated, manually touched up. The PI discounted them for exactly this reason — "manual labels also have
   inaccuracies in them". Optimising against them on the few labelled subjects would fit annotation error.
4. **The denominator is not what a reader assumes.** The `gmwm` Dice uses the full OCT class count in the
   denominator, so it collapses toward zero when label coverage under the block is low. I62's reported Dice of
   **0.0** is an artefact of `labels4` being the tiny BA-only label for that subject (no whole-hemisphere label
   exists for I62 at all), compounded by only **37.3 %** of its BA labels landing on MRI tissue.
5. **Label–tissue overlap is independently broken on several subjects.** Only **6.56 %** of I57's BA labels and
   **57.9 %** of its whole-hemisphere labels land on MRI tissue; I48 is at 64.2 % / 62.7 %; I56's
   `tissue_fraction` is **0.9886**, meaning its tissue mask calls essentially everything tissue and any
   tissue-overlap sanity check on it is vacuous. Read this as a caution on the *metric*, not as a diagnosis of
   the run — in particular I48's "uncertain" verdict comes from its 0.0013 search-score margin, not from its
   label coverage, and its Dice is unusable in both directions rather than merely deflated.
6. **Dice is insensitive to the one error the structural objective cannot see.** The depth-axis scale is off by
   roughly 17 % in the structure-only I46 solution, and Dice barely moves across the entire vascular correction
   that fixes it: **WM 0.8010 → 0.8026** while the scale goes 1.026 → 1.219.

#### 3.5.3 What counts as real evidence, ranked

| Tier | Evidence | Why it is strong | Current status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Independent annotation not used in fitting, scored as a distance** | manual MRI vessel points pushed into the OCT vessel EDT. It has a measurable ceiling and a control | I46 `vessels_vesseg`: median **265 → 167 µm**, f150 **0.283 → 0.473** across the vascular stage, against a ±3 mm random-shift control at ≈352 µm / f300 0.43. The oracle *fitted to those same annotations* tops out at f150 **0.466**, so 0.473 **is** the annotation ceiling — you cannot do better against a single-voxel line annotation |
| 2 | **An independent anatomical prior the registration never saw** | every DANDI OCT block is `sample-BrocaAreaS01`, so the registered block **must** contain the BA label. Cheap, brutal, and requires nothing new | I46: **12.8 %** of BA voxels inside the block, centroid **9.6 mm** away. I55: **59.0 %**, **7.8 mm**. I38 / I56 / I62: **0.0 %**, centroid **57.4 / 65.2 / 60.5 mm** away |
| 3 | **Convergent independent estimates of a physical quantity** | different data, different people, same number | depth scale 1.1667 (sibling metadata) / 1.17419 (authors' affine) / 1.177 (oracle) versus our automatic 1.14–1.24 |
| 4 | **A reverse control on a sibling subject** | it predicts a *null* result and gets one | I55, whose metadata is correct: depth stretch **0.913**, vascular stage moves the block only **0.334 mm**, 8/8 restarts within 0.3 mm. **Downgrade this tier when quoting it:** I55's recovered depth-to-in-plane anisotropy is 0.8570 ≈ 6/7, the exact inverse of the 7/6 factor I46 is missing, so the null may not be independent of the thing it is controlling for (§3.4.4) `[OPEN]` |
| 5 | **Cross-validation of an oracle** | it distinguishes fitting from measuring | 3 seeds × 2 folds split by vessel connected component: held-out oracle f150 **0.42** versus in-sample 0.466 |
| 6 | **Visual QC** — checkerboards, edge overlays, block-location panels | necessary, and the PI's preferred development signal | done for all runs. **Caveat that must stay on the record: the approved figures were generated by an agent and no human has verified them yet** |
| — | **Restart consistency** | **explicitly not a correctness test** | see below |

**Restart consistency deserves the explicit warning.** The runs with the *tightest* restart scatter are among
the ones the human marked **wrong**: **I58 and I61 both converge 12/12 within 0.5 mm** and both are wrong. A
stable wrong basin is still wrong.

**Correction:** several older project documents put **I57 at 12/12** in that list. **I57 is 10/12** — its
corner-mean min/median/max is **0.381 / 0.388 / 0.536 mm**, so two restarts exceed the 0.5 mm gate and 12/12 is
arithmetically impossible. The full set, read from `evaluation.restarts` in each `result.json` (all `n = 12`):
I38 12, I46 9, I48 11, I55 9, I56 10, I57 10, I58 12, I61 12, I62 11, `xiangrui_I58bs` 10,
`xiangrui_I58bs_novasc` 10. **The argument survives on I58 and I61; drop I57 from it.**

#### 3.5.4 The honest scoreboard

| subject | visual verdict | quantitative support | what the independent checks say |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I46** | correct | **yes** — vessels and labels | vessel f150 at the annotation ceiling; 12.8 % of BA inside the block |
| **I55** | correct | **yes** — the strongest single result in the project | 59.0 % of BA inside the block, centroid 7.8 mm; Dice 0.921 / 0.930 |
| I38 | correct (visual only) | **no** | MRI vessel annotation **55.2 mm** away; 0.0 % of BA inside; OCT-WM lands on MRI GM about twice as often as on MRI WM. Note also that its *structural* depth scale, 0.861, is exactly the clamp bound `exp(−0.15)` — the optimiser hit the wall, so that number is saturated, not measured |
| I56 | correct (visual only) | **no** | **65.9 mm** / 0.0 % of BA; 0/8 vascular restarts; tissue mask calls 98.9 % of the volume tissue |
| I62 | correct (visual only) | **no** | **58.6 mm** / 0.0 % of BA; only the tiny BA label exists, so its Dice of 0.0 is a label-coverage artefact and not a statement about the pose |
| I48 | uncertain | — | search top-1 **0.2571** vs top-2 **0.2558** — a margin of **0.0013**, and that thin margin is the *whole* basis of the "uncertain" verdict. Its Dice is untrustworthy in **both** directions and cannot be used to argue either way. **Do not** file I48 with I62 and the other large slabs: their problem is label coverage, I48's is that nothing separates its top two candidates |
| I57 | **wrong** | — | **no explanation** `[OPEN]`. It is *not* the tissue-mask failure it has often been filed as: its threshold 15.77 sits **above** its median intensity 13.80, `tissue_fraction` is a normal **0.209**, and a histogram valley was found (`valley_ratio` 0.0631). Whatever breaks I57 is something else, and nobody has found it |
| I61 | **wrong** | — | **this one is** a tissue-mask failure: threshold 6.80 against a median of 10.42, `tissue_fraction` **0.742**, no histogram valley at all. The mask swallows the bath |
| I58 (DANDI) | **wrong** | — | registered against the **10°** flip (`flip-3`); the 30° volume is on disk, so re-running is a free experiment |
| I58 brainstem (own) | coarse correct | **none possible** | no labels exist. The residual described as "a few millimetres, larger toward the deep end" is a **visual estimate only**; no artefact quantifies it `[UNVERIFIED]` |

**How far the tissue-mask diagnosis actually reaches.** It is the most over-applied explanation in this project,
so state its scope every time you use it. Read from `work/<SUBJ>/prep.json`, the mask is genuinely broken on
exactly **three** subjects — **I56** (threshold 3.62 against a median of 15.15, `tissue_fraction` 0.9886, no
valley), **I58** (threshold 2.12 against a median of 16.93, fraction 0.587, no valley) and **I61** (threshold
6.80 against a median of 10.42, fraction 0.742, no valley). In each the Otsu split lands below the tissue mode
and the mask absorbs the bath. It does **not** cover **I57**, whose threshold sits above its median, whose
fraction is a healthy 0.209 and whose histogram has a clear valley — I57 fails for a reason nobody has
identified `[OPEN]`. It does not cover **I48** either, whose problem is a 0.0013 search-score margin. Note that
of the three genuine mask failures, one (I56) is nonetheless marked visually correct, so a broken mask is not by
itself a prediction of failure.

So **3 of 9 DANDI subjects currently fail** (I57, I58, I61 — this is 3 of **9**, not "3 of 8" as some older
prose says; nine subjects were run). And the defensible summary statement is: **two subjects with
quantitative agreement, three more that look right but are contradicted by two independent annotation checks,
one uncertain, three wrong, and one own-data pair placed coarsely with no number at all.**

The three visual-only cases (I38, I56, I62) are **the single most important open question in the results** and
must be resolved before any of them is reported as a success. The concrete first check costs minutes: open
`results_inspection/I38_otsu/{mri_region,oct_in_mri_region,mri_labels_region}.nii.gz` in Freeview and look at
whether the BA label patch is anywhere near the slab.

Two further honesty caveats a successor must carry:

- **Runtime, corrected.** Per-subject end-to-end wall time over the nine DANDI otsu runs is **18.7 – 131.1 min**
  (1,124.7 / 1,278.8 / 1,789.8 / 2,019.7 / 2,222.9 / 2,242.6 / 2,263.2 / 2,831.3 / 7,864.1 s), not the
  frequently-quoted "15–40 min"; only 4 of 9 fall inside that range. The 7,864 s outlier is I38, where the
  vascular stage alone took 5,696.8 s. The per-branch timing breakdown is in chapter 6, What we found, and what
  it means.
- **`I46`'s headline numbers are not reproducible with the code currently on disk.** Five of the nine headline
  runs predate the current source: `register.py` mtime **2026-08-20 23:30**, `prep_subject.py` **15:11**,
  `vascular.py` **19:31**, against `result.json` mtimes I46 10:23, I38 19:48, I55 20:18, I56 21:07, I62 22:01.
  I46 is the only subject whose prep *and* registration both predate the current code, and the adaptive overlap
  gate did not exist when it ran (`overlap_gate: null`). The tree is **unversioned** — there is no git history
  anywhere for `octreg`, verified by direct inspection of the compute server — so the exact revision that
  produced `I46_otsu` is **unrecoverable**. A re-run with today's code is the only way to get a comparable
  number, and it should be expected to differ. Chapter 10, State of play: where everything is, records the file
  mtimes this rests on.

#### 3.5.5 The evaluation that still needs to be built

For unlabelled data — which is what the lab's own specimens are, and what all future specimens will be — the
only proposal on record is: **ask for about 20 matched anatomical points annotated on both modalities, roughly
30 minutes of work per pair, and report target registration error.** This **has not been requested from the
PI**. It is on the critical path in chapter 11, What to do next, and it is precisely the gap between "the
figures look right" and a number a reviewer will accept.

Two further requirements fall out of the 2026-08-23 meeting and apply to this project as much as to the
reconstruction side:

1. **State explicitly which data participated in fitting and which only in scoring.** The `vessels_own` channel
   is the channel the vascular stage *optimises*, so `vessels_vesseg` (the DANDI manual segmentation) is the
   honest number for I46. Reporting `vessels_own` as evidence would be circular.
2. **Do not report a metric whose normalisation you cannot defend** — see the `gmwm` denominator problem in
   §3.5.2 #4.

---

### 3.6 How the lab's two projects fit together

The lab runs two workstreams. The split was the PI's, proposed in Slack on **2026-06-02**, seven weeks before
the newer project had a lead.

**Scope contrast, in prose.** (a) is **slice-to-volume within one modality**: reconstruct an isotropic volume
from deformed single-axis, anisotropic LSFM serial sections (I45, then I48), propagate the same deformation onto
discrete cortical-layer labels, and evaluate all of it with no isotropic ground truth to score against. (b) is
**partial-to-whole across two modalities**: find where a 3-D OCT block sits inside a whole-hemisphere ex-vivo MRI
and recover an anatomically plausible affine. One qualifier belongs on the scientific side rather than the
organisational one: `octreg v1` is label-free, training-free and **prior-*optional*** — not prior-free — because
the PI has a position prior in practice (§3.4.8, and §3.7 item 1).

The full side-by-side of the two — leads, advisor, members, inputs, method state, numbers on record, venue, and
the status verdict to use for each — is **not** repeated here. It is chapter 9, The lab: people, history, and the
constraints that shape this work, §9.3.1, with the dated history of the split in §9.3.2; chapter 2, Orientation
and glossary, §A.2 carries only the name-and-metric decoder. What follows is what only this chapter can say: why
one specimen produces both problems at once, and what (a) genuinely hands (b).

**Why the same data serves both, physically.** Look again at §3.3.2. The 500 µm slab the vibratome removes *is*
the LSFM specimen, and the block it was removed *from* is the OCT volume. **One specimen, one cutting operation,
produces both problems at once** — the shavings for project (a) and the remaining block for project (b). That is
also why DANDI:000026 carries all three modalities for the same participants: `ses-SPIM` 38,735 assets /
34.25 TB of LSFM, `ses-OCT` 51 assets / 133.4 GB, `ses-MRI` 1,577 assets / 1.58 TB. We hold **0.17 %** of the
dandiset and **none** of the LSFM.

**How they relate as work.** Costantini et al. solved OCT↔LSFM per slice, in 2-D, using the OCT block face as
the reference (§3.3.3). Project (a) is attacking the harder version — reconstruct *across* slices **without**
that reference — which is why NeSVoR was ruled unsuitable for a single-axis stack but explicitly reserved for
the follow-up in which OCT and MRI supply genuinely different reference volumes. Project (b) owns the other end
of the chain. **Neither project's output is the other's input today.**

What (a) genuinely supplies to (b) is a set of lessons and assets rather than data: reconstructed volumes that
could enter a 3-D registration later; failure modes it has already exposed (pairwise drift, non-uniform physical
space, provenance accidents); the layer labels and boundary metrics; and — most usefully — the evaluation
philosophy. Lavanya's own unprompted self-audit on 2026-08-23, that an NCC of 0.99 should prompt a check for
whether the same images were used for both fitting and scoring, generalises **directly** to this project's
vessel channel (§3.5.5 item 1).

---

### 3.7 What a newcomer must not claim

These are the places where the record is genuinely ambiguous and where anyone writing outward-facing text will
otherwise overstate. The full risk register is chapter 12, Open questions and unverified claims; this is the
short list, with the corrected numbers.

1. **Do not call the whole-hemisphere prior-free search the project's value proposition.** The PI has a position
   prior in practice (§3.4.8). Frame it conditionally: use the prior when it is given, search when it is not.
2. **Do not write "5 of 9 subjects verified correct"** without the qualifier that only **I46 and I55** have
   quantitative agreement, and that three of the remaining "correct" verdicts are contradicted by two
   independent annotation checks.
3. **Do not quote the 1.174 / 1.177 / 1.22 depth-scale agreement as a target registration error.** It is a
   comparison of scale *magnitudes* derived in two different coordinate conventions. No sub-millimetre ground
   truth exists for this data — see §3.4.5, last row.
4. **Do not treat restart consistency as a correctness check** (I58 and I61 are 12/12 and wrong).
   **Do not substitute an absolute NCC threshold for it either.** `refine.final_ncc` does not separate right
   from wrong across subjects: I61 scores **0.5020** and I57 **0.5121** and both are wrong, while I62 scores
   **0.2842** and is visually correct. Any "a good result scores above X" rule stated on that field is refuted
   by its own corpus.
5. **Do not report the brainstem residual as "a few millimetres"** as though it had been measured. It is a
   visual estimate with no artefact behind it.
6. **Do not describe the rough anatomical prior as a precise ROI or set of coordinates** — nobody has said what
   it is `[OPEN]`.
7. **Do not claim novelty for** coarse-to-fine affine, FFT translation search, Frangi vesselness, Otsu
   thresholding, local-mean bias correction, MIND-SSC, or the idea of using vessels as the cross-modal landmark.
   All are prior art, and the vessel idea is the baseline's own. The defensible one-line framing is: *we removed
   two human inputs — the annotations and the position prior — from an existing validated pipeline, and showed
   that the one thing lost, the depth-axis scale, can be recovered from automatically segmented vasculature.*
8. **Do not assert that a smoother-looking result is anatomically more accurate.**
9. **Do not quote "154 s for a whole hemisphere" for the label-free pipeline** — that figure comes from the
   `--features mixed` parser-probability configuration of `run_demo_i46.py`. The label-free number is **299 s**
   per polarity branch, **598 s** as the wrapper actually runs it (§3.4.3).
10. **Do not cite the 33-slice section period as evidence about I46's depth spacing.** That line of argument is
    withdrawn; it breaks on I56 (§3.4.6). The depth-spacing case has three legs, not four.
11. **Do not present I55 as an unqualified independent null.** Its recovered depth-to-in-plane anisotropy is
    0.8570 ≈ 6/7, the exact inverse of the factor I46 is missing, and nobody has shown that is a coincidence
    (§3.4.4). Likewise, do not quote I38's structural depth scale 0.861 as a measurement — it is the clamp
    bound `exp(−0.15)`, i.e. saturated.
12. **Do not attribute I57's failure to its tissue mask.** Its mask is fine; the failure is unexplained
    `[OPEN]`. The mask diagnosis covers I56, I58 and I61, and only those (§3.5.4).

Finally, the methodological hole this project sits in, from the lab's own literature review: **no public,
peer-reviewed benchmark exists for a human, centimetre-scale 3-D OCT block, of unknown position, registered back
into a whole-hemisphere MRI with independent target-registration-error annotation.** That absence is
simultaneously the opportunity and the reason every number in this document had to be argued for from first
principles rather than looked up.

## 4. The data

Two data sources exist and only two. Everything the project has ever run on comes from one of them.

| source | where it lives on the compute box | size | labels? |
|---|---|---:|---|
| DANDI:000026 (Costantini et al. 2023) subset, 9 subjects | `~/autodl-tmp/oct-mri-registration/data/costantini/dandi-000026/` | 64,730,457,001 B (60.28 GiB) in 97 files | yes, on the MRI side |
| Xiangrui Zeng's own I58 brainstem pair | `~/autodl-tmp/oct-mri-registration/data/xiangrui/OCT_to_MRI/` | 13,117,697,928 B (12.22 GiB) in 2 files | **none** |

Combined: **77,848,154,929 B = 72.50 GiB, 99 files.** `du -sh` on the two trees reports `61G` and `13G`.

The asymmetry between those two rows is the whole reason the project is organised the way it is. The public
dataset is the only place where an OCT block, a whole-hemisphere MRI of the same brain, *and* manual
annotations to score against all exist together. The lab's own data is the target the PI actually cares about
and it has no annotations at all. So DANDI is where the method is developed and validated, and the brainstem
pair is where it is applied and where its accuracy can only be argued, never measured.

---

### 4.1 What DANDI:000026 is

| field | value |
|---|---|
| Title | "Human brain cell census for BA 44/45" |
| DANDI ID | `DANDI:000026`, version `draft` |
| Paper | Costantini et al., *A cellular resolution atlas of Broca's area*, **Sci Adv 9, eadg3844 (2023)**, published 12 October 2023 |
| Authors' code | <https://github.com/neuroscales/biccn-broca-I46>, tag `1.0`, commit `b36e398cc42db4ca89ecc121818255bd96fc67ad`, Zenodo DOI `10.5281/zenodo.7832049` |
| Licence | CC-BY-4.0 |
| BIDS version | `1.0` claimed at the top level, `1.5.0` inside the derivative datasets — inconsistent |
| Funding | NIMH `1U01MH117023` (a BICCN grant) |
| Participants | **20** in `participants.tsv` (sex and age only): EXC022, I38, I41, I45, I46, I48, I52, I53, I55, I56, I57, I58, I59, I60, I61, I62, I63, I64, HCPA1, KC001 |
| Full draft size, measured 2026-08-23 | **40,982 assets, 38,464,536,222,290 B = 34.98 TiB** |
| What we hold | **0.17 %** of it |

**`draft` is mutable.** There is no published version tag. Asset UUIDs, sizes and even paths can change under
you. A spot-check on 2026-08-23 against the live listing confirmed that four pinned UUIDs (`f5a098f4…` I38
EPIC flip-2, `b686f4c2…` I46 OCT, `67b968b1…` I58 OCT, `a7204687…` I46 wholehemi) still resolve to the same
path *and* the same byte count, so the draft had not drifted since the 2026-08-19 capture — but that is a
fact about one week, not a guarantee.

**Why this dataset and not another.** It is the only public dataset that carries the exact modality pair this
project registers (serial-sectioning OCT block ↔ ex-vivo whole-hemisphere 7 T MRI of the same specimen) with
manual segmentations on the MRI side to score against, and whose authors also published their own
registration recipe — so the same dataset supplies the validation data *and* the baseline method it is
compared against (see chapter 8, How this compares to the published method). The PI confirmed in the
2026-08-14 meeting that the public dataset ships manual segmentation, which is what makes a Dice number
possible at all.

| `ses-` | assets | bytes | what it is |

| `ses-SPIM` | 38,735 | 34.25 TB (31.15 TiB) | light-sheet / confocal LSFM (custom inverted confocal light-sheet), `.ome.tif` chunks, stains `Calretinin`, `NeuN`, `Calbindin`, … 10 subjects |
| `ses-Hip-CT` | 6 | 2.49 TB (2.27 TiB) | hierarchical phase-contrast synchrotron volumes, **sub-I58 only**, 3 `.ome.zarr` chunks of 1023.4 / 921.0 / 548.7 GB |
| `ses-MRI` | 1,577 | 1.58 TB (1.44 TiB) | 7 T ex-vivo whole-hemisphere MRI (raw multi-echo VFA FLASH + B1 maps) plus the `EPIC` derivative |

`.ome.tiff` 92 / 76.0 GB.

Note the shape of that table. **99.8 % of the dandiset by volume is LSFM and synchrotron CT, neither of which
this project touches.** The OCT session — the thing the whole project is about — is 0.4 % of it. That is why
a 72 GiB working subset is enough.

#### 4.1.2 The MRI: VFA multi-echo FLASH, and the EPIC derivative

Acquisition, read from the BIDS sidecars (all identical in kind): Siemens **MAGNETOM Terra**,
`MagneticFieldStrength 7`, `InstitutionName "MGH, HST"`, `PulseSequenceType "GRE"`, `RepetitionTime` 0.034 s
or 0.045 s, `FlipAngle` 10 / 20 / 30 deg. It is a **variable-flip-angle (VFA) multi-echo FLASH** protocol.

Two directories per subject matter:

* **Raw** — `sub-XX/ses-MRI/anat/sub-XX_ses-MRI_echo-{1..4}_flip-{1..3}_VFA.nii.gz` (12 files for I46, 16 for
  I58), plus a B1+ transmit map series `sub-I58_ses-MRI_flip-{1..16}_TB1DAM.nii.gz`. Each raw echo volume is
  2.6–4.9 GB. **We downloaded none of these.**
* **`derivatives/EPIC/`** — the only MRI we use. Its `dataset_description.json` says: B0 distortion
  correction by the **EPIC** method (Varadarajan et al., "Edge-preserving B0 inhomogeneity distortion
  correction for high-resolution multi-echo ex vivo MRI at 7T"), then FreeSurfer `mri_ms_fitparms` with the
  B1+ transmit fieldmap, producing *synthesised* per-flip contrasts corrected for B0 and B1+ inhomogeneity.
  Per subject it contains `sub-XX_ses-MRI_flip-N_VFA.nii.gz` plus quantitative maps named either
  `sub-XX_ses-MRI_{PD,T1,T2star}_VFA.nii.gz` or `sub-XX_{PDmap,T1map,T2starmap}.nii.gz` — the naming is
  inconsistent *between subjects*.

Why the correction machinery matters to us: the readout gradients are **bipolar**, so odd and even echoes are
distorted in opposite directions wherever B0 is inhomogeneous, and the echoes misalign. The MRI we register
against is therefore a **derived, corrected, synthesised FLASH contrast**, not raw scanner output. Anyone who
wanted to work from the raw echoes would have to re-implement EPIC plus `mri_ms_fitparms` first.

**`flip-N` is an index, not an angle.** This is the single most quoted-wrong fact about this dataset. The
`FlipAngle` field of `sub-I58_ses-MRI_flip-1_VFA.json` is `"30"`; of `sub-I58…flip-3` it is `"10"`; of
`sub-I57…flip-4` it is `"20"`. The index-to-angle map differs per subject and **must** be read from the
sidecar. Registering I58 on `flip-3` — a 10° VFA FLASH with almost no GM/WM contrast — is why the I58 run
failed. (Authority note: the project's older operations notes state this **inverted**, as `flip-1 = 10°` /
`flip-3 = 30°`. That is wrong. The sidecars are the truth: `cat` the two files in
`~/autodl-tmp/oct-mri-registration/data/costantini/dandi-000026/derivatives/EPIC/sub-I58/ses-MRI/anat/` and
`sub-I58_ses-MRI_flip-1_VFA.json` reads `"FlipAngle": "30"`, `sub-I58_ses-MRI_flip-3_VFA.json` reads `"10"`;
`work/I58/prep.json → mri.file` confirms the pipeline used `flip-3`. The *conclusion* that no 20° acquisition
exists for I58 is nevertheless correct. The correction is also logged in chapter 12, Open questions and
unverified claims.)

#### 4.1.3 OCT naming, and the distinction that matters most

The canonical path is

```
sub-XX/ses-OCT/micr/sub-XX_ses-OCT_sample-BrocaAreaS01_OCT.ome.tiff
```

* **`sample-BrocaAreaSNN` identifies the tissue specimen.** `samples.tsv` (79 data rows, columns
  `sample-sample_id`, `participant_id`, `sample_type`) lists `BrocaAreaS01…S23` plus `MotorCortexS01…S08` for
  sub-I46 (31 rows) and `BrocaAreaS01…S48` for sub-I48 (48 rows). **Every other participant has zero rows.**
* **Only `sample-BrocaAreaS01` is published as a reconstructed OCT volume**, one per subject — verified across
  all nine `work/<SUBJ>/prep.json` files. So the real operational task for a specimen is placing *many*
  pieces, and the public data lets you practise on exactly *one* per subject.
* **Plain `*_OCT.ome.tiff` = the already-reconstructed, stitched, downsampled volume.** One file per subject,
  1–10 GB, a single-resolution uncompressed TIFF stack, one page per z-slice. **This is what `octreg`
  consumes.**
* **`acq-Raw` + `.ome.zarr` = raw, un-stitched tiles.** There is exactly **one** such asset in the entire
  dandiset: `sub-I48/ses-OCT/micr/sub-I48_ses-OCT_sample-BrocaAreaS23_acq-Raw_OCT.ome.zarr`,
  **54,116,961,443 B (50.40 GiB)**, plus a 573-byte sidecar. Note the block number: **S23, not S01.** It is
  not the raw form of any volume we hold, there is no reconstructed S23 volume, and there is no MRI-space
  label for it — so it cannot be registered at all. We deliberately did not download it (§4.7).

Confusing the two is the classic first-day mistake. Everything the pipeline assumes — a rigid 3-D array with
one spacing triple, a single tissue mask, an affine from array indices to a physical frame — is true of the
plain OME-TIFF and false of the zarr. The zarr's only value is that its `.zattrs` carries **per-tile stage
coordinates**, which is why fetching a few kB of metadata from it (not the 50 GiB array) is the cheapest way
to settle what a "sample" physically is for I48 (§4.9, [OPEN]).

Two further OCT-side directories:

* `derivatives/Depth_normalized_OCT_volume/<SUB>/…` — depth-attenuation-corrected copies of the same blocks,
  20 assets, 36.1 GB. The naming there is a mess: I38/I45/I48/I57/I60 use `*_depth-normed_OCT.ome.tiff`, I55
  uses `*_depth-corrected_OCT.ome.tiff`, and I58/I59/I61/I62 use plain `*_OCT.ome.tiff` (byte size differing
  from the raw-session copy by a handful of bytes — so a filename alone will not tell you which one you have).
  **We downloaded none of these**; `octreg` does its own per-slab normalisation.
* `derivatives/sub-XX/ses-OCT/vessel/ves_seg.tif` — manual/semi-automatic **OCT-side** vessel segmentation.
  Exists for **only 5 subjects**: I38, I45, I46, I48, I60.

#### 4.1.4 Label naming

```
derivatives/Labels/sub-XX/ses-MRI/anat/sub-XX_ses-MRI_space-EPIC_label-<X>_dseg.nii.gz
```

with `<X>` one of:

| `<X>` | what it is | values |
|---|---|---|
| `infrasupra` | GM/WM plus the infragranular/supragranular boundary, **inside BA 44/45 only** | 1 / 2 / 3 |
| `infrasupra_seg-wholehemi` | the same 3-class scheme propagated to the **whole hemisphere** | 1 / 2 / 3 |
| `vessels` | manual MRI vessel label | **not standardised** — see §4.4.3 |

Provenance, from `derivatives/Labels/dataset_description.json`: manual drawing on every 10th slice +
**SmartInterpol** (<https://github.com/aleatzeni/SmartInterpol>) + manual touch-up. The sidecars carry a
single key, e.g. `{"Source": "sub-I46_ses-MRI_flip-2_VFA.nii.gz"}` — that names the MRI the labels were drawn
on, and it **does not always match the flip we registered against** (§4.4.1).

`prep.json → oct.tissue_frac150`; "MRI tissue cm³" is `prep.json → mri.tissue_fraction` × the MRI's own FOV
volume. All figures re-read from the nine `prep.json` files on the compute box on 2026-08-24.
