## 5. The method, as a chain of reasoning

`octreg v1` is not an assembly of registration techniques picked off a shelf. It is close to the unique shape
you get when you take "register a small 3-D block into a big 3-D volume" and impose four constraints that were
all observed in this data *before* any code was written, plus one organisational constraint that decides
several of the arguments outright. Read the constraints first; everything after them is a consequence, and
almost every apparent design freedom disappears once they are on the table.

| # | Constraint | The measurement that establishes it | What it forbids |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C-cross** | The two modalities share no intensity scale. OCT is optical backscatter; MRI is a synthesised VFA FLASH contrast. | Direct cross-modality intensity NCC, 20 µm OCT vs 0.08 mm MRI: **0.033** at a 0.32 mm level, **0.030** at 0.16 mm (`scripts/test_polish.py`, `logs/test_polish.log`). Optimising that similarity moved a pose the human had judged correct by **9.37 mm** centre / **15.79°** / **9.55 mm** corner-mean. | Any objective that assumes a fixed intensity relationship between the two images. |
| **C-prior** | The block can come from anywhere in the hemisphere, at any orientation, in either handedness. | **6 of 9** DANDI runs are mirrored — I38, I46, I48, I56, I58, I62; not mirrored: I55, I57, I61 and both brainstem runs (`final_transform.mirror` of all nine `result.json`, confirmed by the `mirror` column of `work/runs/summary_all/summary.md`). Block centres range over ±40 mm on every world axis. | Any method that needs the answer's neighbourhood as an input. |
| **C-meta** | The metadata lies, and there is no second record to catch it. | I46's OME-TIFF sidecar declares 12 µm isotropic. Four independent lines say the depth spacing is 14–15 µm: sibling sidecars are 12×12×14 and 30×30×35 (ratio **1.1667**); the authors' hand-drawn-vessel affine has largest-axis scale **1.17419**; an oracle affine fitted to manual labels + manual vessels in our frame gives **1.177**; our own vessel channel recovers **1.219**. (A fifth candidate line — the measured 33-slice serial-section period against a 500 µm vibratome cut — was examined and **withdrawn**; see chapter 4, The data, §4.8.3 for why it does not survive I56.) | Trusting a voxel size. The geometry has to be recoverable from the images. |
| **C-scale** | 0.77–1.43 **G** voxels of MRI and 1–5 G voxels of raw OCT, on **one RTX 4090 with 24 GB**. | I46 MRI 1280×1040×576 = 767 M voxels; I38/I57/I61 1600×1400×640 = 1.43 G; I46 OCT 627×1271×1230 = 980 M; the brainstem OCT 1457×2013×1595 = 4.68 G (13.0 GB on disk). | Anything that materialises a full-resolution float32 pair on the GPU. |
| **C-nolabels** | The data the project exists for has no annotations at all. | Xiangrui's I58 brainstem pair is exactly two files, `I58_Brainstem_mus_Slice_full_20um_corr.nii.gz` and `I58_brainstem_MRI_cropped_to_OCT.nii.gz`. No labels, no segmentations, no vessel annotations, no reference transform — that directory, `~/autodl-tmp/oct-mri-registration/data/xiangrui/OCT_to_MRI/` on the compute server, contains those two files and nothing else. | Anything that needs an annotation *to run*. Such a thing is a method for DANDI:000026, not a method for this project. |

C-nolabels is the one that most often settles an argument. It is why the trained parser is not shipped (§5.6),
and it is why the DANDI manual annotations are quarantined into evaluation only and never enter the objective.

### 5.0 The core idea

The one-sentence statement, from `EXPLAINER_zh.md` §2:

> Translate both modalities into the same language — a white-matter / grey-matter two-class map — do the global
> match in that common language; hand the last part that tissue geometry cannot determine (sub-millimetre and
> the depth scale) to the vessels.

Underneath that sentence is a second organising principle, and it is the cleanest way to describe the whole
pipeline to someone in one breath: **every discrete unknown is enumerated, every continuous unknown is
optimised, and nothing discrete is ever left to a gradient.** Translation, rotation, handedness and class
polarity are enumerated at 0.6 mm; scale and shear are optimised, late, under an explicit prior; the depth
scale is opened up only once a channel exists that can see it.

The four stages, with what each is allowed to know:

| Stage | Question it answers | Representation it works on | DOF it may change | Typical cost (I46) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Structure maps** | What do these two volumes have in common at all? | raw MRI + raw OCT → 2-channel WM/GM probability maps + a tissue mask on each side | none (it is a representation, not a solve) | seconds–minutes, mostly CPU |
| **Global search** | Where in the hemisphere is the block, in which orientation, in which handedness? | 0.6 mm two-class maps, masked NCC via FFT | 3 translation + 3 rotation + handedness (discrete) + polarity (discrete, decided later) | **298.9 s per polarity**, 597.8 s with both |
| **Affine refinement** | Given that pose, what is the best 12-DOF fit the structure supports? | 0.6 → 0.3 → 0.15 mm two-class maps, masked NCC, Adam | +3 log-scale, +3 shear, under `reg = 2.0` and clamps ±0.15 | 388.4 s per polarity, including its share of the search |
| **Vascular refinement** | What is the depth-axis scale, which structure cannot see? | 3-channel: WM, GM, and a vessel channel; clamps ±0.3, `reg = 0.5` | all 12, with the scale prior relaxed | 158.3 s |

The two entry points map onto this directly: `scripts/prep_subject.py` builds every cached representation into
`work/<SUBJ>/`, and `scripts/register.py` runs stages 2–4 and writes `work/runs/<run>/`. Nothing else is on
the live path. `LEVELS = (0.6, 0.3, 0.15)` mm is hard-coded in `register.py`, as are `scales=(1.0,)` for the
search, `log_every=4000`, the refinement schedule, the restart magnitudes, the count of 8 vascular restarts,
and the choice of `mri_dark_channel` for the MRI vessel channel.

One provenance caveat that must travel with every number in this chapter. The tree is unversioned — there is
no `.git` anywhere under `~/autodl-tmp/oct-mri-registration` — and **five of the nine headline DANDI runs
predate the current source**:
`register.py` has mtime 2026-08-20 23:30, while `result.json` for I46 (10:23), I38 (19:48), I55 (20:18),
I56 (21:07) and I62 (22:01) are all earlier. I46 is the only subject whose prep *and* registration both
predate the current code. The revision that produced `I46_otsu` is unrecoverable, and the adaptive overlap
gate — `overlap_gate: null` in `work/runs/I46_otsu/result.json` — did not exist when it ran. The reasoning
below is sound; the exact reproduction of I46's headline numbers with today's code is `[OPEN]`.

---

### 5.1 Structure maps: why both modalities are reduced to a two-class WM/GM map

#### 5.1.1 The problem

C-cross says there is no intensity correspondence to exploit. But the *anatomy* is identical — the same piece
of fixed tissue was imaged twice — so the job is to find a representation that (a) both modalities can produce
independently, (b) depends on tissue identity rather than on how it was imaged, and (c) is cheap on 1 G voxels
and simple enough to be correlated by FFT. Clause (c) is not decoration; §5.2.2 shows that it is what makes
the exhaustive search affordable, and therefore what makes C-prior survivable.

Why WM/GM is the right common language: WM and GM differ in myelin content, which changes both optical
scattering and T1. In serial-sectioning OCT, WM is one roughly uniform brightness and GM is another; in ex-vivo
FLASH at 20°, likewise. *Which* of the two is brighter is a protocol property and flips between subjects
(§5.2.5) — but that there are two roughly uniform classes with an anatomically-shaped boundary between them is
stable across both modalities. The cortical folding pattern is then the signal, and folding is a property of
the tissue, not of the scanner.

#### 5.1.2 The alternatives, and what each was actually worth

| Alternative | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Raw intensity**, tissue-z-scored, sign-flipped by polarity (`features.build_features(kind="intensity")`) | Tried; works on I46 but the basin is half as reliable; actively harmful on our own data | I46 crop: search top1 **0.594** vs otsu's **0.727**; refined NCC 0.693 vs 0.753; restarts **4/8** vs 7/8 (`work/runs/crop_intensity_v2/result.json`, `work/runs/runs_summary.json`). On the brainstem pair it is worse than useless: NCC 0.03, and optimising it dragged a correct pose 9.55 mm (C-cross). |
| **MIND-SSC** — the standard training-free cross-modality descriptor (Heinrich 2013), implemented faithfully in `features.py::mind_ssc` | Tried, **total failure** | I46 crop: search top1 **0.219** against otsu's 0.727, and the refinement *lowered* it to **0.185** — the optimiser walked away from its own starting point. 3/8 restarts. The block landed 17.9 mm centre / 33.0 mm corner-max from the reference, with **0** manual MRI vessels inside it (`work/runs/crop_mind_v2/result.json`, `logs/run_crop_mind_v2.log`). Reading: MIND's local rotational and contrast invariance discards exactly the large-scale class-layout signal this problem lives on, and a 12-channel local descriptor evaluated at 0.6 mm on a cortical block is nearly texture-free. **Do not revisit without a fundamentally different descriptor.** |
| **Mutual information** — the textbook multimodal answer (Wells/Viola/Maes 1997) | **Never implemented, never measured on this data** | The lab's own review names its two failure modes for exactly this problem: MI "does not encode spatial structure, is not global localization" (`literature_review/working/classical_partial_methods.md:318`) and "histogram estimation and capture range are sensitive to small overlap" (`:317`). Overlap here is ~1 %: I55's OCT mask is 5.4 cm³ against 620.5 cm³ of MRI tissue, which is **0.87 %** (computed here from the two recorded volumes). But the decisive argument is structural, not empirical: **MI is not a sum of products, so it does not factor through an FFT.** Choosing MI would have cost the exhaustive search, i.e. it would have cost C-prior. If a reviewer asks "did you try MI?", the honest answer is **no** — a masked-MI multi-start affine is baseline B1 in the lab's review and has not been run. |
| **A learned cross-modal descriptor / segmenter** | Built, works, deliberately not shipped | §5.6. |

#### 5.1.3 Why the two-class map wins, in order of weight

1. **It is the only option that survives C-cross and stays FFT-able.** A per-channel probability map in `[0,1]`
   is a plain array; masked NCC over it is a sum of products; sums of products are correlations; correlations
   are FFTs. MI is not FFT-able at all. MIND is (12 channels, ~6× the cost) but carries no signal here.
2. **It is invariant to the thing that actually varies.** Masked NCC on the class map is invariant to any
   affine intensity transform *per channel*, so the absolute calibration of neither modality matters — only
   the shape of the WM/GM boundary, which is the object both scanners agree about. This also means the two
   sides' sigmoid sharpness does not have to be calibrated against each other (§5.2.3).
3. **It costs nothing to produce.** Otsu plus a tissue mask; no training, no annotation, seconds of compute.
   The entire argument of §5.6 is that a far more expensive representation buys the same registration.

#### 5.1.4 What it costs — say this out loud

Reducing to two classes throws away every intra-class gradient. That loss is not free, and it is precisely
what §5.4 is about: a two-class cortical block is *geometrically degenerate* along one axis. The method
concedes the loss and buys the missing axis back from a different channel, rather than pretending the
structural objective can see it. Anyone presenting this method should state the concession before someone else
does.

#### 5.1.5 Bias-field flattening before Otsu, and what breaks without it

**The problem.** Otsu is a *global* threshold. It assumes the histogram of the whole volume is bimodal with
the two modes corresponding to the two classes. An ex-vivo whole-hemisphere FLASH acquisition violates that:
receive-coil sensitivity produces a smooth multiplicative field across the specimen, so WM near the coil can be
brighter than GM far from it. The modes smear together and one global cut is wrong almost everywhere.

Measured on I46: the local tissue mean over the hemisphere runs **p5 = 29.328, p50 = 36.606, p95 = 55.382** —
a **1.9× intensity ramp across the specimen**, which is larger than the WM/GM contrast the threshold is
supposed to be measuring.

**The alternatives.**

| Alternative | Why not |
|---|---|
| Local/adaptive Otsu per patch | Works, but makes the class assignment position-dependent, so it is no longer a single consistent labelling — and it is expensive on 1.4 G voxels. |
| N4 / ANTs bias correction | A dependency, a second parameter set, and slow on a whole hemisphere. v1's entire design intent is as few moving parts as possible. |
| Learn the segmentation instead (the U-Net branch) | Sidesteps the bias field entirely — and this is exactly the comparison that killed the U-Net (§5.6). |
| **Divide by the local tissue mean** (shipped) | Classic retrospective/homomorphic correction. Not novel — the project says so plainly. The *measured effect* is the contribution. |

**The choice, exactly.** `features.py::otsu_two_class_lowmem` does this before any thresholding:

```
pool  = 4
num   = pool_mean_np(vol * tissue, 4)                      # tissue-only, pooled
den   = pool_mean_np(tissue, 4)
field = gaussian_filter(num, σ) / (gaussian_filter(den, σ) + 1e-3),   σ = 10 mm / (vox_mm · 4)
field = max(field, max(0.5 · percentile(field[den > 0.5], 5), 1e-3))  # floor: division cannot explode
```

and then thresholds `vol / field`. Three details carry meaning:

- **σ = 10 mm is a physical 10 mm** (§5.7): 16.67 pooled voxels at 0.15 mm, 20.8 at 0.12 mm. Stated that way
  it invites the question "is a receive-coil bias field really smooth at 10 mm?", which has a physical answer.
  Stated as "σ = 16.67 voxels" it invites nothing.
- **The `den` denominator is what makes it a *tissue* mean rather than a volume mean.** Air and bath do not
  drag the field down at the specimen edge, so the correction does not invert near the boundary.
- **The floor** on `field` is what makes division by a small number impossible in the low-signal periphery.

Then: threshold from a `[::3,::3,::3]` subsample of `vol/field` inside tissue, clipped at its 99.5th
percentile; `thr = threshold_otsu(sub)`; `scale = 0.25·std(sub)` for the sigmoid.

**The evidence** (re-derived first-hand on 2026-08-23, I46 against `work/I46/labels4.npy`, replicating the
function exactly — pool 4, σ = 10 mm/(0.15 mm × 4) = 16.67 pooled voxels, field floored at 0.5 × p5, Otsu on a
`::3` subsample clipped at p99.5, 1-voxel pre-blur, `mri_wm_bright = False`):

| Arm | Otsu threshold | Dice WM | Dice GM |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Raw intensity, no flattening | 44.5918 | **0.6502** | **0.5987** |
| Divided by the local tissue mean, σ = 10 mm | 1.0292 | **0.9069** | **0.9343** |

**This improvement is confirmed.** It was re-derived first-hand from the raw MRI and the manual labels rather
than copied forward from a document, and the two arms above are the precise figures. `octreg/README.md` quotes
**0.66/0.62 → 0.90/0.93**, which is the rounded pair to use in prose; every README figure agrees with the
re-derivation to ≤ 0.02, the residual being nearest-neighbour vs trilinear field upsampling and a hard vs
sigmoid threshold. The one thing worth knowing about its provenance is that no artefact produced by the
pipeline itself ever contained these numbers, so the re-derivation *is* the record — reproduce it with
`/root/miniconda3/envs/octmri/bin/python -u /tmp/flat.py I46 0.15` on the AutoDL box (~4 min, CPU,
read-only).

**Why this one step carries the whole label-free claim.** Without flattening, a training-free two-class MRI map
agrees with manual labels at Dice **0.66/0.62** — that is not a segmentation, it is a coin flip with a bias. At
that quality the central argument of §5.6 ("a trained U-Net gives the same registration, so ship the untrained
one") would be false, and the method would need labels, and it would then not be a method for the lab's own
data at all (C-nolabels). The operator is 1980s-standard; the measured fact that it lifts a plain Otsu to Dice
**0.90/0.93** on a whole hemisphere is what makes the label-free branch viable.

**One more thing it buys.** Flattening is what makes the polarity flag safe. The run `crop_final_inv2` fed a
*tissue-inverted* MRI and still recovered the pose (depth stretch 1.145; vessels 179–182 µm / f150 0.438–0.441,
indistinguishable from the non-inverted 179–181 µm). A global Otsu on an un-flattened volume would not have
been stable under that. Caveat to keep with it: `crop_final_inv2` recorded **0/12** structural restarts
converged, and its re-parsed twin `crop_final_inv2_w` recovered 8/12 — polarity handling is functional but the
restart basin is fragile.

#### 5.1.6 The histogram peak-walk tissue threshold, and why a naive threshold was not enough

**This is a different job from §5.1.5.** Flattening + Otsu splits *tissue* into WM and GM. The peak-walk
threshold splits the field of view into **foreground (tissue) vs background (air, embedding fluid, MR bath)**.
It matters more than it looks, because everything downstream is masked by it: the Otsu statistics are computed
inside it, the search's overlap gate is defined by the ratio of two volumes derived from it, and the OCT
block's own mask determines what the search template even is.

The ex-vivo whole-hemisphere FLASH histogram is **not bimodal**. It has up to three modes: air near zero,
bath/fixative fluid (low but nonzero, and *large* in volume), and tissue. A two-class cut puts the bath on
whichever side happens to win.

**Three generations, recorded in `EXPLAINER_zh.md` §5:**

1. **Plain Otsu.** Pulled off target by bright artefacts — a single bright inclusion moves the between-class
   variance optimum.
2. **Three-class multi-Otsu plus a valley test.** Better, but I38's histogram has a real, deep valley *between
   air and bath*; multi-Otsu reported it, the valley test accepted it, and the bath was admitted as tissue.
3. **Peak-walk** (`common.py::histogram_tissue_threshold`), shipped:
   - clip above the **99.5th percentile** (outlier suppression — the fix for generation 1);
   - 256-bin histogram smoothed with `uniform_filter1d(size=5)`;
   - `find_peaks(prominence = 0.05·max, distance = 5)`;
   - take the **rightmost** peak as the tissue mode;
   - walk **left** across prominent peaks and cut at the first valley whose depth ratio
     `h[valley] / min(h[left_peak], h[tissue_peak])` is below **`deep = 0.5`**;
   - if no such valley exists, fall back to `min(p1, 0.5 · multiotsu3[0])` (or `percentile(sub, 10)` if
     multi-Otsu throws), i.e. keep essentially everything.

**The design idea is a shift of anchor.** Generations 1 and 2 asked "where is the best cut in this histogram?"
— a question about the whole histogram, and therefore hostage to every mode in it. Generation 3 asks "starting
from the tissue mode, how far left can I go before I fall off a cliff?" — a question about the tissue mode
only. Anchoring on tissue is what stops a bright artefact or a large bath mode from stealing the anchor.

**The evidence, including that it is still not enough.** `prep.json → mri.{n_peaks, peak_pos, valley_ratio,
tissue_fraction}` is the diagnostic trail, and it is already written for every subject. The full nine-subject
panel — threshold, tissue fraction, valley ratio, mask volume, search scores and verdict side by side — is in
chapter 7, Failures, dead ends, and things that bit us, §7.1.1; read it there rather than have it twice. What
this section needs from it is the spread, and one number the rest of the document depends on.

**The expected volume of a hemisphere, measured rather than remembered.** Computing
`mri.shape × mri.voxel_mm³ × mri.tissue_fraction` from each `work/<SUBJ>/prep.json` on the compute server gives
the mask volume the pipeline actually used. Six subjects produce a mask that could plausibly be a fixed
hemisphere: **I48 386.3, I57 518.0, I62 531.5, I55 620.5, I46 802.9, I38 805.8 cm³.** That measured band —
**386–806 cm³**, established and derived once in chapter 4, The data, §4.3 — is the only "expected hemisphere
volume" this document uses; where a threshold is derived from it below, it is derived from the **806 cm³** top
of that band and from nothing else. Three subjects fall
grossly outside it: **I58 1 453.4 cm³** (`tissue_fraction` 0.587, `n_peaks: 1`), **I61 1 838.8 cm³** (0.742)
and **I56 2 519.0 cm³** (0.9886) — roughly 1.8×, 2.3× and 3.1× the largest plausible hemisphere mask in the
set. All three have `valley_ratio: null`.

I61 is where the consequence is clearest. Its 0.6 mm two-class map contains a large field of homogeneous bath,
and a 21 cm³ block finds a comfortable, repeatable, meaningless correlation maximum inside it: search top1
0.5172, refined NCC 0.5020, **12/12** restarts converged, and the block sits **95.7 mm** from the labelled
hemisphere. It is not in the brain. The same mask failure is present on DANDI-I58 (compounded there by a 10°
flip angle with no GM/WM contrast to correlate) and on I56, where the mask is almost the whole field of view
and the real anatomy nevertheless won the search.

**Say plainly which subjects this diagnosis covers.** It covers **I61, DANDI-I58 and I56**, and no others.
It does **not** cover I48, whose mask is the *smallest* in the set at 386.3 cm³ and whose "uncertain" verdict
rests on a search margin of 0.0013, not on its mask. And it does **not** cover **I57**: I57's threshold is
15.77 against an intensity median of 13.80 — the threshold sits *above* the median, which is what a working
tissue cut looks like — its `tissue_fraction` is 0.209, squarely inside the healthy band, its mask volume is
518.0 cm³, and the peak-walk rule found a real valley at **0.0631**. Every diagnostic this section proposes
passes on I57, and I57 is still wrong. **I57's failure has no explanation `[OPEN]`.** Any table or heading that
files I57 under "tissue-mask failure" is wrong and should be corrected.

**The design lesson, stated as a criticism.** The fallback **fails open**: when the rule cannot find a valley it
keeps everything, writes `valley_ratio: null` into `prep.json`, and proceeds. That is the wrong default for a
method whose robustness story is "nothing fails silently". `valley_ratio: null` is a good leading indicator —
it fires on all three mask failures — with one false alarm (I55, where the fallback fired and the run landed
correctly anyway) and one blind spot (I57, which has a valley at 0.0631 and fails regardless). It is not a
missing field on the healthy subjects either: I46 records **0.1161**, I38 **0.1984**, I62 **0.0869**, I48
**0.4737** — the worst separation in the set, barely clearing the `deep = 0.5` gate. The v1.1 fix has two
halves, both already scoped:

- a **volume sanity gate** — reject when the "tissue" volume exceeds 1.5× the top of the measured band, i.e.
  **1.5 × 806 ≈ 1 210 cm³** (chapter 4, The data, §4.3). Derived from that 806 cm³ maximum and nothing else,
  that single line clears all six plausible masks and catches I58 (1 453), I61 (1 839) and I56 (2 519);
- a **texture-based** foreground mask, because bath and tissue differ in texture, not in mean intensity.
  Exploratory code exists (`scripts/test_texture_mask.py` → `work/texture_mask_test.png`). Note that
  `EXPLAINER_zh.md` §4 records that *pure* texture thresholding was tried and **failed on both datasets** — the
  fix is texture **fused with** intensity, not texture instead of it.

Neither half would have saved I57.

This is the same problem family as the agarose case on our own data (§5.2.3), which is why the project treats
the MRI bath mask, the OCT agarose mask and the anti-artefact fine channel as **one** problem — foreground
separation — and makes it the definition of v1.1.

#### 5.1.7 The OCT side of the representation

Three OCT-specific decisions belong in this stage.

**(a) Slab normalisation, because serial-sectioning OCT has a periodic depth attenuation.** Each 500 µm
vibratome cut has its own attenuation profile, so the reconstructed stack carries a sawtooth along the depth
axis. `common.oct_slab_normalize` removes it: per z-slice, `med[i] = median(slice[slice > tissue_thresh])`
computed only when more than **2000** voxels pass; NaNs interpolated over z; `ref = uniform_filter1d(med,
size=window)`; `scale[i] = ref[i]/med[i]`; output slice = `raw[i]·scale[i]·gain`. Slow trends (real tissue
variation) survive because they appear in both `med` and `ref`; the sawtooth is divided out.

`window` is meant to be one section period, set as `window = max(10, int(round(1200.0 / sp[0])))` with the
in-code comment `# ~1.2 mm of depth = one section period at 12 um`. **That comment is wrong by roughly 3×.**
Measured by FFT and autocorrelation of the per-slice in-tissue median on the raw OME-TIFFs, the period is
**33 slices** for I46 against a window of 100, and **12 slices** for I56 against a window of 34 — 3.03 and
2.83 periods respectively. The full table, with the FFT peaks, the autocorrelation lags and harmonics and the
`period × spacing` products, is in **chapter 4, The data, §4.8.3**, where the section period belongs.

I46 survives by luck — 100 ≈ 3 whole periods, so the running mean averages an integer number of sawteeth. I56's
window is 2.83 periods, so a residual sawtooth survives into the normalised volume. The brainstem pair's
`slab_window = 60` at 20 µm has never been measured `[UNVERIFIED]`. The correct fix is not a different
constant: it is to **measure the period per subject** (the autocorrelation is ten lines) and set `window` to
the nearest integer multiple. `[NOT RE-MEASURED]` in the latest audit pass — the period measurement itself
comes from decoding the raw OME-TIFFs and was not repeated; re-run `/tmp/period.py` on the box to confirm.

**One thing this measurement is not.** The section period was once tried as a route to the I46 depth-scale
correction — 500 µm of vibratome cut ÷ 33 slices — and it is **withdrawn**, because the identical arithmetic on
I56 contradicts a sidecar that is corroborated twice inside the file. The counter-example is worked through in
**chapter 4, The data, §4.8.3**. The measurement is sound and it matters for `window`; it says nothing
reliable about voxel spacing, and it is not one of the lines of evidence in the C-meta row above.

**(b) The sigmoid softness.** `features.otsu_two_class` blurs by σ = 1.0 voxel, takes
`thr = threshold_otsu(x[tissue])` (median if fewer than 100 tissue voxels; 0 if none), and forms
`s = sigmoid((x − thr)/scale)` with **`scale = 0.25·std(vals)`**. A hard threshold would make the NCC gradient
zero almost everywhere, which matters because the same maps are used by a gradient-based refinement; a quarter
of a standard deviation is soft enough to give gradient across the WM/GM boundary and hard enough that the map
still looks like two classes. Because masked NCC is invariant to a per-channel affine intensity change, the
fact that the OCT and MRI sides pick different `scale` values from their own statistics is harmless — the
sharpness cancels.

**(c) Polarity-agnostic channel ordering.** `register.py` builds the OCT features once as
`FO_bright_first, thr_o = otsu_two_class(oct150, MO.bool(), wm_bright=True)`, i.e. **channel 0 is always the
brighter class**. Polarity is applied later by swapping (`FO_bright_first[[1,0]]`). That is what makes running
both polarities cost one extra search rather than one extra feature build, and it keeps a single definition of
"channel 0" in the cache.

The block's registration grid itself is built physically: `k150 = max(1, round(target_mm·1000/sp))` per axis
(anisotropic integer pooling), then resampled onto an **exactly isotropic `--target-mm` grid in the same
frame** — so I46's 627×1271×1230 at 12 µm becomes `shape150 = (49, 100, 97)` at 0.15 mm, and the brainstem's
1457×2013×1595 at 20 µm becomes (194, 267, 212). The OCT tissue mask is `oct_tissue_mask`: threshold →
`binary_closing(iterations=2)` → `binary_fill_holes` → **largest connected component only**.

---

### 5.2 Global search: why exhaustive, and how it is made affordable

#### 5.2.1 Why exhaustive rather than a local optimizer with an initialization

**The problem is C-prior.** The baseline (Costantini 2023, `mri2oct_affine.sh`) requires the MRI to be
**pre-cropped by a human** to roughly where the block came from, then walks `--progressive` t→r→s→a from
identity. That is a good method for refining a known pose. It is not a method for *finding* a block.

The failure of a local optimizer here is not gradual. A gradient-based affine on a cortical block in a whole
hemisphere, started from the wrong gyrus, does not land slightly off — it lands on a different gyrus. Cortex is
self-similar at the scale of a 15 mm block, so the objective has an enormous number of local optima and the
basin of attraction of the true one is roughly one gyrus wide.

Worse, two of the four unknowns are **discrete**, and no continuous optimiser can cross either:

- **handedness** (§5.2.4): `det(T[:3,:3]) < 0` is a separate connected component of GL(3); a gradient step can
  never reach it from a proper rotation without passing through a degenerate matrix;
- **class polarity** (§5.2.5): swapping the two channels is a discrete relabelling.

So a local optimizer would need not one initialization but 4 × (however many gyri), and would still have no way
of telling you that it had missed.

| Alternative | Why not |
|---|---|
| Human crop box (the baseline) | It is the human input we are trying to remove, and it is the *only* human input in the baseline that cannot in principle be produced by a script — the labels could be automated; the crop box is a judgement about where the tissue was taken from. |
| Multi-start local optimization (e.g. NiftyReg Aladin multi-start; baseline B1 in the lab's review) | Gives K answers and no denominator: you never learn whether the pose space contained a better one. It also cannot cross the two discrete branches. |
| Keypoint/descriptor matching + RANSAC | Requires repeatable keypoints across the two modalities. C-cross says the intensity relationship is arbitrary, and MIND (§5.1.2) shows local descriptors carry nothing here. |
| Learned pose regression | Needs training data of exactly the kind that does not exist for the target specimens (C-nolabels). |

**The choice.** At 0.6 mm, score **every** translation (via FFT) × **8 000** quasi-uniform SO(3) rotations ×
**{proper, mirrored}** = **16 000 orientations**, then keep the top **24** after non-maximum suppression in
pose space. NMS declares two poses duplicates only if their block centres are within `min_sep_mm = 3.0`
**and** their rotations within `min_sep_deg = 10.0°` — both, not either. `random_rotations` covers SO(3) via
normalised random quaternions with **`R[0]` forced to the identity**, so the untransformed orientation is
always tried. `scales=(1.0,)` is hard-coded: the search does not search scale, and §5.3 explains why that is
deliberate rather than an omission.

Worked out here from the recorded grid sizes, how many poses this actually scores: I46's padded 0.6 mm grid is 360×300×184, of which
322×262×146 = **12.3 M translations** are valid (template fully inside). × 16 000 orientations =
**1.97 × 10¹¹ poses per polarity**, × 2 for `--oct-wm-bright auto` = **3.9 × 10¹¹ poses per subject**, in
2 × 299 s.

**A note on the default that will bite a successor.** `register.py:32` declares
`--oct-wm-bright choices=["auto","yes","no"], default="no"`. **`auto` is not the default** — every DANDI run
got it because `run_subject.sh` line 21 hard-codes `--oct-wm-bright auto`. Someone calling `register.py`
directly will silently get single-polarity behaviour, and, given §5.2.5, a coin-flip chance of a ~70 mm error.

#### 5.2.2 The complexity argument: why FFT is what makes exhaustivity affordable

Masked NCC at every translation needs, per orientation, these correlation maps between the padded MRI grid and
the rotated template (`search.py::score_rotation`): `SI[c]` (2), `SII[c]` (2), `overlap` (1), `STI[c]` (2) =
**7 correlation maps** for C = 2 channels.

**Direct evaluation** costs `N_grid × n³` multiply-accumulates per map. For I46 the 0.6 mm MRI level is
320×260×144; `template_n = 39`; `pad = n//2 + 1 = 20`, so the padded grid is 360×300×184 = **N = 1.99 × 10⁷**
and `n³ = 59 319`.

**FFT evaluation.** `FI[c] = rfftn(I[c])`, `FI2[c] = rfftn(I[c]²)` and `Ftis = rfftn(tissue)` are transformed
**once, before the rotation loop** — that is the entire trick. Per orientation you then need 3 forward
transforms (`rfftn(w)`, `rfftn(w·T[c])` × 2) and 7 inverse transforms = **10 FFTs** of an N-point grid.

Counted here with the conventional 5·N·log₂N flop model:

| | Per orientation | × 16 000 orientations |
|---|---:|---:|
| Direct | 7 · N · n³ = 8.25 × 10¹² MAC = 1.65 × 10¹³ flop | 2.64 × 10¹⁷ flop |
| FFT | 10 · 5N log₂N = 2.41 × 10¹⁰ flop | 3.85 × 10¹⁴ flop |
| **Ratio** | | **≈ 690×** |

The measured I46 search is **298.9 s per polarity** (`work/runs/I46_otsu/result.json → search.seconds`), so
597.8 s for both. At 690× the same work done directly is **≈ 57 hours per polarity**, ≈ 4.7 days per subject.
That is the difference between a method and a thought experiment.

The structural statement: **the FFT replaces an O(n³) inner product per translation with an amortised O(log N)
per translation, so the template's size drops out of the per-translation cost entirely.** That is why the
design can afford to score bigger blocks — I57's `template_n = 128` would be 35× more expensive per translation
than I46's 39 in the direct formulation, but costs the same FFTs.

Two consequences that shaped the rest of the code:

1. **Search time scales with the MRI grid, not with the block.** The brainstem's 0.08 mm crop (0.6 mm grid
   42×61×61) takes **44.8 s**; I46/I55 whole hemispheres at 0.15 mm (grid 320×260×144) take 298.9 / 430.9 s;
   the 0.12 mm subjects take 604.8–1 010.3 s. `template_n` ranges 39 → 128 across these and barely matters.
   Corpus range: **44.8 s – 1 010.3 s per polarity**.
2. **The FFT dictates the representation.** Masked NCC is FFT-able because it is a sum of products; MI is not.
   Had the project chosen MI, exhaustive search would have been unaffordable and C-prior would have had to be
   conceded. **The representation choice and the search strategy are one decision, not two.**

**Timing hygiene.** Do not quote "150 s for a whole hemisphere". A real, logged 153.4 s / 153.7 s
full 16 000-orientation search exists (`logs/run_whole_final.log`, `logs/run_whole_final2.log`), but it comes
from `run_demo_i46.py --features mixed`, i.e. **MRI channels that are a trained 3-D U-Net parser's
probabilities**, on a different prep directory (`work/i46`, lower case). It is not the label-free path. The
honest sentence: *an exhaustive 16 000-orientation search over all translations costs 45 s on a 0.08 mm
brainstem crop and 299 s on a 0.15 mm whole hemisphere with the label-free Otsu features (154 s with the
parser-probability features); the shipped wrapper runs it once per class polarity, so budget 598 s of search
for a whole hemisphere.* Related: the 4 000-orientation tick is **75 s** for I46 and ranges 11 s (brainstem) to
254 s (I57) across the corpus; 150 s/4000 is true only for I58. And 76 s vs 154 s is not "superseded" —
`whole_mixed_real` (8 000 orientations) and `whole_final2` (16 000) are the same code at half the count,
exactly 2× apart.

#### 5.2.3 Why masked NCC, computed only inside the block mask

**The problem.** The template is a tiny fraction of the target. I55's OCT mask is 5.4 cm³ against
620.5 cm³ of MRI tissue — **0.87 %**, computed here from the two recorded volumes. A similarity computed over any fixed window would be dominated by the
~99 % of the window that has no OCT counterpart at all.

There are three distinct things "masked" has to fix, and they are usually conflated:

1. **Which voxels contribute.** Only OCT-tissue voxels. Everything outside the block mask is not evidence about
   anything — the OCT simply does not observe it.
2. **What the mean and variance are computed over.** This is the subtle one. If the statistics are computed
   over a fixed window while the summation is masked, the normalisation is wrong and the score stops being
   scale-invariant. Both `search.py::score_rotation` and `refine.py::masked_ncc` compute `ma, mb, va, vb` with
   the mask weights `w` — mean and variance are properties of the *masked* sample.
3. **Comparability across poses with different overlap.** This is Padfield's point, and it is why the
   normalisation is called overlap-normalised: `N = w.sum()`, every moment is divided by it, so a pose hanging
   half off the specimen is neither automatically penalised nor rewarded. It is scored on what it covers and
   then admitted or rejected by a **separate explicit gate**.

Separating "score the pose" from "is the pose admissible" is what lets admissibility be a hard, interpretable
threshold instead of a soft penalty nobody can defend.

**Why NCC rather than SSD.** The two class maps are sigmoid probabilities with different sharpness — the OCT
side uses `0.25·std` of the OCT tissue values, the MRI side `0.25·std` of its own. There is no reason for those
to match. Masked NCC is invariant to `a → αa + β` per channel, so the arbitrary sharpness of each side's
sigmoid cancels. SSD is not, and would need a calibration step with no justification behind it.

**The overlap gate, and why it had to become adaptive.** This is the one place in the document where the gate
is written out in full; everywhere else it is referred to, not restated. `min_overlap = 0.85` says: at least 85 % of the
template's mass must land on MRI tissue. Poses failing it are set to **−2.0** before the argmax. Then our own
data broke it. In OCT, **agarose embedding scatters like tissue** — `logs/prep_xiangrui.log` records
`raw tissue thr 0.0` and `oct150 tissue frac 0.779`. The OCT "tissue" mask (28.9 cm³) is more than twice the
cropped MRI's tissue (13.3 cm³), so the best achievable overlap is ≈ 13.3/28.9 = 0.46 and a fixed 0.85 gate
**rejects every pose in the space**. `register.py:111`:

```python
MIN_OV = float(min(a.min_overlap, max(0.15, 0.8 * V_m / max(V_o, 1e-6))))
```

Read it as: the effective gate is the requested `min_overlap`, or 80 % of the best overlap the two mask
volumes physically permit, whichever is smaller — but never below 0.15. The `0.8` is a safety margin below the
theoretical ceiling; the **`0.15` floor** stops the gate from disappearing entirely on a specimen whose OCT
mask dwarfs its MRI tissue. **Always quote the formula with the floor** — several prose documents drop it, and
without it the expression says something the code does not do. Observed values
(`result.json → overlap_gate`): **effective = requested = 0.850 on all eight DANDI runs that record it** — the
gate never binds on DANDI — and **0.369** on the brainstem pair (V_mri_tissue 13.3 cm³ vs V_oct_mask 28.9 cm³).
`work/runs/I46_otsu/result.json` has `overlap_gate: null` because the gate did not exist when it ran.

The principle worth carrying beyond this project: **a threshold on a ratio of two measured volumes should be
expressed as a fraction of the achievable maximum, not as an absolute constant.** An absolute constant encodes
an assumption about the data — that the two masks measure the same object — which our own specimen violates.

#### 5.2.4 Why mirror / handedness must be searched

**The problem.** A microscopy stack's handedness relative to physical space is not guaranteed. Two independent
mechanisms produce a flip: the block can be physically turned over on the vibratome, and the stack's storage
order (which array axis increases in which physical direction) is a convention of the acquisition software, not
a measurement. Nothing in an OME-TIFF tells you which happened. Verified from all nine `result.json`:
**6 of 9 DANDI runs are mirrored** — I38, I46, I48, I56, I58, I62 — while I55, I57, I61 and the brainstem pair
are not. (README.md and EXPLAINER_zh.md both say "5 of 9" and name the wrong set; the verified count is 6 and
**I48 is the one that gets dropped** from the list. Fix the docs.)

**Why it cannot be handled anywhere else.** `det(M) < 0` is a *different connected component* of GL(3). A
gradient-based optimiser parameterised by a rotation vector cannot reach it — the determinant would have to
pass through zero, i.e. the block would have to be collapsed to a plane, which the loss and the scale clamps
both forbid. Handedness is therefore not a hard optimisation problem; it is a **discrete branch that must be
enumerated somewhere**, and the search is the only stage that enumerates anything.

The implementation is one line in `search.run`:

```python
if mirror: Rs = np.concatenate([Rs, Rs @ np.diag([1.0, 1.0, -1.0])], 0)
```

plus one supporting decision in `common.py`: `rotation_geodesic_deg` **returns a hard 180.0 when
`det(R1 R2ᵀ) < 0`**. Poses of opposite handedness are declared "not comparable", which is exactly what makes
NMS treat a proper and a mirrored candidate as always distinct — a mirrored pose can never suppress a proper
one out of the top-24. Without that, the two branches would compete for candidate slots and one would starve.

`refine.py` then carries the branch forward as a **fixed boolean**, not a parameter:
`M = R(r) · Shear(sh) · diag(exp(ls)) · [diag(1,1,−1) if mirror]`, with `mirror` read once by
`params_from_matrix` from `det(A) < 0` and never optimised. That is correct: the search decided it; the
refinement must not be able to un-decide it by sliding through a degenerate matrix.

**The evidence.** `crop_mixed_nomirror` — I46, which *is* mirrored — run with `--no-mirror`:

| | with mirror | `--no-mirror` |
|---|---:|---:|
| search top1 | 0.7328 | **0.6848** |
| refined NCC | 0.7307 | **0.6853** |
| Dice WM / GM | 0.798 / 0.829 | **0.767 / 0.806** |
| vessel median | 297 µm | 284 µm |
| recovered scale | — | degenerates to **[0.955, 1.0, 1.0]** |

Note the tell in the last row. Denied the correct handedness, the optimiser does not fail loudly; it finds a
plausible-looking wrong pose with a degenerate scale vector. That is the signature of a discrete branch being
wrong, and it is why the branch is not left to chance.

**The cost, stated honestly.** Exactly **2× the search**: 16 000 orientations instead of 8 000. Since the
search is only 8–38 % of wall clock (the vascular stage dominates), doubling it to remove a ~50 %-probability
failure mode is not a close call.

#### 5.2.5 Why class polarity cannot be decided by the coarse search, but can by the refined NCC

**The problem.** `otsu_two_class` produces two channels: bright and dark. Which one is WM is a **protocol
property** — it depends on the OCT acquisition (attenuation-corrected µs vs raw backscatter, wavelength,
contrast convention) — and it changes between subjects *within the same dataset*. I46's winning polarity is
GM-bright; I55's is WM-bright; I38's WM-bright; I56's GM-bright. Nothing in the sidecars records it.

**Why the coarse search is structurally blind to it.** This is a genuine symmetry argument, not a numerical
accident. At 0.6 mm, a cortical block's two-class map is **a sheet of GM wrapped around a core of WM**. Swap
the two class labels and you get a sheet of "GM" wrapped around a core of "WM" again, with the roles of the two
sides of the boundary exchanged. Somewhere else in the hemisphere, at a different fold with the opposite local
curvature, there is a place where that inverted sheet fits just as well. At 0.6 mm the representation is smooth
enough that "sheet of A around a core of B" is essentially all the information there is, so the two polarities
are near-degenerate.

**The evidence, which is unusually clean.** `work/runs/I46_parser_wrongpol_v0/result.json` is the
wrong-polarity branch run to completion and kept deliberately as a demonstration:

| | correct (`I46_parser`) | wrong polarity |
|---|---:|---:|
| **search top1 (0.6 mm)** | 0.7273 | **0.7275 — higher** |
| **refined NCC (0.15 mm)** | **0.7218** | 0.7136 |
| block centre (mm) | −5.55, 25.91, 8.53 | 4.54, −41.89, 27.50 (**≈ 70 mm away**) |
| Dice WM / GM vs manual labels | 0.803 / 0.824 | **0.857 / 0.772 — WM Dice higher** |
| `frac_on_mri_labels` | 0.999 | 0.991 |
| manual MRI vessels inside the block | 4 970 | **0** |
| vascular vessel-channel NCC | **0.301** | **−0.035** |
| vascular restarts ≤ 0.3 mm | 8/8 | **0/8** |

Three separate warnings live in that table, and they should be read slowly:

1. **The coarse search score is worse than useless here** — it is 0.0002 *higher* at a pose 70 mm from the
   truth.
2. **Dice against manual GM/WM labels is also worse than useless** — the wrong pose scores a *higher* WM Dice
   (0.857 vs 0.803). Same symmetry: a swapped two-class sheet lands where the label sheet is also swapped.
   **Anyone using label Dice as their primary endpoint on this problem will confidently accept the wrong
   answer.**
3. **The refined NCC separates them, and the vessel channel separates them decisively.**

For the shipped `otsu` features on the same subject the separation is wider: refined NCC **0.7564 vs 0.7300**
against coarse search **0.7259 vs 0.7411** — again the wrong polarity wins the coarse search
(`logs/reg_I46_otsu.log` lines 7 and 12). Cross-subject: I55 refined 0.746 vs 0.506; I38 0.478 vs 0.226.

**Why the refined NCC *can* decide it.** Three things change between the 0.6 mm search and the 0.15 mm refined
score, and all three break the symmetry:

- **Resolution.** At 0.15 mm the map is no longer "a sheet": it has sulcal shapes, WM tract branchings, local
  cortical thickness variation. Those are chiral in the class labelling — the geometry on the WM side of the
  boundary genuinely differs from the geometry on the GM side.
- **12 degrees of freedom.** The refinement can locally fit; a wrong-polarity pose has to fight the boundary
  curvature rather than ride it.
- **It is a fit quality, not a match count.** The search score says "there exists a plausible place"; the
  refined score says "and this is how well a full affine actually fits there".

**The choice.** `--oct-wm-bright {auto, yes, no}`. `auto` runs the search *and* the refinement for **both**
polarities and keeps `min(trials, key=lambda k: trials[k]["best"]["loss"])`, i.e. the higher refined NCC wins.
Cost: exactly 2× the structural stage (I46: 2 × 388.4 s). Against a 70 mm error that *every structural metric
endorses*, this is the cheapest insurance in the pipeline. When the protocol is known, pass `yes`/`no` and
halve the cost. Each trial is logged under `polarity_trials.{False,True}` with `search_top1/2, refined_ncc,
centre, mirror, seconds`, so the decision is auditable after the fact.

**And keep the independent check.** The vessel-channel NCC (**0.301 vs −0.035**, 8/8 vs 0/8 vascular restarts)
is an *independent* verifier: it is not part of the objective the polarity decision was made with. That is the
single strongest reason to keep the vascular stage even where its geometric effect is small — on I55 it moves
the block only 0.334 mm, but `ncc_channels[2] = 0.083` still confirms the pose.

#### 5.2.6 What exhaustivity buys, and what it does not

**It buys, first, the removal of the human input.** That is contribution #1, and it is the reason the method
transfers to a specimen nobody has ever registered before.

**It buys a certificate with a denominator.** Because every pose at 0.6 mm was scored, `top1` and `top2` are
global statements. The margin `top1 − top2` is therefore meaningful in a way no multi-start result can be, and
it carries the project's one hard operating rule (`EXPLAINER_zh.md` §4): **search margin < 0.01 ⇒ a human must
look at the figure.** The rule has teeth:

| Run | top1 | top2 | margin | Verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| I46 | 0.7259 | 0.7039 | 0.0220 | correct |
| I55 | 0.6112 | 0.6089 | 0.0023 | correct (the rule would flag it) |
| Xiangrui I58bs | 0.1247 | 0.1184 | 0.0063 | coarse correct |
| I48 | 0.2571 | 0.2558 | **0.0013** | **uncertain** |
| I58 | 0.2896 | 0.2895 | **0.0001** | **wrong** |

**It buys the discrete branches for free** — handedness and polarity are just more things to enumerate once you
have decided to enumerate.

**It does not buy correctness**, and this is the most common misreading of the result. An exhaustive search
returns the global optimum *of the objective you gave it*. If the objective is wrong — a tissue mask containing
1 839 cm³ of bath — the global optimum is confidently, reproducibly wrong. Two consistency checks confirm this,
and both are traps:

- **Restart consistency is not a correctness test.** The runs with the *tightest* 12-restart scatter are among
  the ones the human marked wrong: **I58 12/12 and I61 12/12**, both wrong. (An earlier draft added I57 to
  that list; I57 is **10/12**, with corner-mean min/median/max **0.381 / 0.388 / 0.536 mm** — two restarts
  exceed the 0.5 mm gate, so 12/12 was arithmetically impossible. The argument survives on I58 and I61.)
  Meanwhile the two verified-correct runs, I46 and I55, are **9/12** each. Full set, all n = 12: I38 12,
  I46 9, I48 11, I55 9, I56 10, I57 10, I58 12, I61 12, I62 11, brainstem 10 and 10.
- **Nor is a high score — and no numeric threshold on `refine.final_ncc` will separate right from wrong across
  subjects.** I61's refined NCC is **0.5020** and I57's is **0.5121**, and both poses are wrong; I62's is
  **0.2842** and it is the correct pose. The coarse score inverts the same way: I61 scores top1 0.517 at a
  pose 95.7 mm outside the brain, while I56 scores 0.340 at a pose the human judged correct. **Absolute NCC is
  a within-subject quantity only.** If you write an acceptance rule, it has to be a margin (`top1 − top2`), a
  physical sanity check (mask volume, label containment) or an independent channel (the vessel-channel NCC) —
  never an absolute score, and never a "good result above X" line on `final_ncc`.

What exhaustivity actually does is convert the question "did my optimiser converge?" — unanswerable — into "is
my objective right?" — answerable, by reading `tissue_fraction` and `valley_ratio` out of `prep.json`. That is
real progress, and it is not the whole story: those two fields name the cause of the I61, DANDI-I58 and I56
mask problems, but I57 passes every one of them and its failure is still unexplained `[OPEN]` (§5.1.6).

**And the prior is not worth keeping even when you have it.** `--crop-centre` / `--crop-half-mm` still exist
and were ablated directly:

| Pair | Poses | Search cost |
|---|---|---|
| `crop_mixed_v2` vs `whole_mixed_v2` | identical within noise | — |
| `crop_final` vs `whole_final` | identical | — |
| `crop_final2` vs `whole_final2` | stretch [1.184, 0.973, 1.034] vs [1.195, 0.975, 1.035]; vessels 166.8 µm / f150 0.469 vs 166.6 / 0.474 | 12–14 s (crop, 4 000 rot) → 153 s (whole, 8 000 rot) |

**A 30 mm position prior buys nothing in accuracy and saves about two minutes.** Since producing it costs a
human, v1 runs whole-hemisphere by default. That is the cleanest possible justification for a design choice:
the alternative was implemented, measured, and found to be worth less than its own input cost. (Framing
caveat, from the PI: in practice the lab *does* know roughly where the block came from, so global search is
robustness insurance and a paper capability, not the value proposition. The label-free half of the claim is
untouched by that.)

### 5.3 Affine refinement: the DOF schedule, clamped shears, and a scale prior

#### 5.3.1 The problem

The search hands over a pose with **6 DOF fixed and 6 unknown**: it returns `R` and `t` and hard-codes
`scales=(1.0,)`. Opening all 12 at once, at the finest level, from a coarse pose is the standard way to turn a
nearly-right answer into a confidently-wrong one — the extra 6 parameters absorb a positional error as a
distortion, the loss goes down, and the anatomy goes wrong.

#### 5.3.2 The schedule

| Level | DOF | iters | Candidates in → out | MRI extent used |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| 0.6 mm | rigid, then **similarity** (isotropic scale — the forward pass uses `ls.mean().expand(3)`) | 120 | 24 → 8 | the whole pooled 0.6 mm region |
| 0.3 mm | rigid, then affine | 200 | 8 → 3 | a crop, half = `BLOCK_R + 6` mm around the current pose |
| 0.15 mm | affine | 200 | 3 → 1 | same crop rule |

Two independent things are happening and they should be read separately.

- **DOF opening.** Rigid first (fix the pose); then *isotropic* scale — one parameter, which is the only scale
  question a coarse level can answer; then anisotropic scale and shear, only once the pose is right at 0.3 mm.
  **Anisotropic scale can never be introduced at 0.6 mm, by construction.**
- **Candidate pruning.** 24 → 8 → 3 → 1. Cheap levels evaluate many hypotheses, expensive levels few. That is
  what makes keeping 24 candidates affordable, and keeping 24 is what makes the top-1/top-2 margin a real
  quantity rather than an artefact of a greedy pipeline. A "distinct runner-up" is reported too: the first of
  `lvl015[1:]` that is more than 2.0 mm or 5° from the winner.

Two extra refiners with `half_mm = BLOCK_R + 12.0` are built around the best pose specifically for the
restarts, wide enough to hold a ±30° / ±5 mm perturbation.

#### 5.3.3 The prior, and the sharpest single number in the design

The refinement loss is

```
loss = (1 − masked_NCC) + reg · (Σ ls² + Σ sh²),      reg = 2.0
```

with hard clamps after every optimiser step: `ls ∈ [−0.15, 0.15]` (scale factor **0.861–1.162**) and
`sh ∈ [−0.15, 0.15]`. `ls` is the **absolute** log-scale, not a delta — the search hands over a pure rotation,
so `ls₀ = 0` and the clamp bounds the *total* scale.

Now compare the prior's price against the available evidence, in the same units (the data loss is `1 − NCC`;
the penalty is `2·ln(s)²` per axis):

| Depth scale s | `ln s` | prior cost at reg = 2.0 | Available NCC gain along that axis |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1.075 (the i-axis NCC argmax) | 0.0723 | **0.0105** | the **entire** i-axis NCC range over s ∈ [0.85, 1.30] is **0.021** |
| 1.162 (the clamp, `exp(0.15)`) | 0.150 | **0.0450** | — |
| 1.177 (the oracle's depth scale) | 0.163 | **0.0531** | — |
| 1.219 (what the vessel channel finds) | 0.198 | **0.0784** | — |

That table is worked out here from the loss definition, and it should be read as epistemics rather than
optimisation. The structural stage's prior
charges **0.045–0.078** of loss to reach the true depth scale, while the *total* amount of NCC that a depth
stretch can possibly earn is **0.021**. The optimiser therefore **correctly refuses to stretch**: the evidence
is genuinely weaker than the prior. And note the clamp: `exp(0.15) = 1.1618` is **below** the oracle's 1.177.
**The structural stage is architecturally incapable of reaching the right answer on I46 — by design.** It is
not allowed to guess a parameter it cannot see.

The clamp binds in the other direction on a real subject, and this must be carried into every table that
quotes it. I38's `structural.stretch_ijk` is `[0.861, 0.948, 0.946]`, and **0.861 is exactly `exp(−0.15)`**:
the lower clamp bound, to three decimals. It is the fence, not a measurement. Whatever depth scale I38's
structure was reaching for, it was smaller than the stage was permitted to give, and the recorded value tells
you only where the optimiser hit the wall. **Wherever 0.861 appears for I38, label it clamp-saturated.**

That is exactly why the vascular stage widens the clamp to 0.3 (`exp(±0.3)` = **0.741–1.350**, which contains
1.219) and lowers `reg` to 0.5. With the vessel channel present the arithmetic flips — again working from the
loss definition — because at
`chan_w = [1, 1, 2]` the vessel channel carries weight 2/4 = 0.5 of the objective, so I46's vessel NCC of 0.296
contributes **0.148** — against a prior cost at reg = 0.5 of only **0.0196** for `ln(1.219)`. The evidence is
now **7.5× the prior**, and the stretch is bought.

**The clamps are not tuning constants. They are a statement about what each stage is entitled to know.** This
is the single most defensible design idea in the project and it is worth leading with in a lab meeting.

#### 5.3.4 The evidence that the prior is load-bearing

`scale_probe.py` re-ran the refinement with the prior removed (`reg = 0`, clamps 0.35) and the affine drifts —
the block collapses along the depth axis. The output `work/runs/validate_real/T_free_affine.npy` exists, but
its printed diagnostics were never captured to a log, so the magnitude is **[UNVERIFIED]** — re-run
`scale_probe.py` to recover it. The qualitative behaviour is recorded in the code notes and in chapter 6,
What we found, and what it means, §6.10.3.

**`T0`, first use — the baseline every I46 ablation below is measured against.** `T0` is
`work/runs/crop_mixed_real/T_oct2mri.npy`: the v0 *structural-only* result on the I46 crop, `stretch_ijk =
[1.032, 1.004, 0.971]`, vessel median **276.5 µm / f150 0.254**, sitting **1.362 mm** from the oracle affine.
Every validation run quoted from here to §5.6 starts from it, so a difference between two rows is a difference
in method rather than in starting pose. Chapter 6, What we found, and what it means, §6.10 uses the same `T0`
for the same reason and gives its full row.

The supporting control is more important and is fully recorded. `reg = 0.5, clamp = 0.3` **with no vessel
channel** (the control row of `vessel_channel_refine.json`) reaches 265.8 µm / f150 0.277 and stays 1.240 mm
from the oracle — against T0's 276.5 µm / 0.254 / 1.362 mm. **Loosening the prior alone gains almost nothing.**
That control is what makes the whole vascular argument in §5.4 non-circular: the gain there is the channel, not
the relaxed regularisation.

#### 5.3.5 Other choices in `refine.py` worth knowing

- **Per-parameter Adam learning rates in physical units**: rotation 0.02 rad, translation **0.3 mm**, log-scale
  0.01, shear 0.01, with `CosineAnnealingLR(T_max=iters, eta_min=0)`. Translation in millimetres rather than
  voxels is part of §5.7.
- **`refine` returns the best data loss seen, not the last iterate.** The reported NCC is never worse than
  something the optimiser actually visited.
- **The regulariser is excluded from the returned score** (`best` tracks `data_loss`, not `loss`), so
  `refined_ncc` is comparable across runs with different `reg`. That is what makes the polarity comparison in
  §5.2.5 and every ablation table legitimate.
- **The parameterisation round-trips exactly.** `params_from_matrix` reads `mirror = det(A) < 0`, right-
  multiplies by `MIRROR` if so, then QR-decomposes `A = QU` with signs fixed so `diag(U) > 0`, falling back to
  `polar_rotation` if `Q` comes out improper, with scales floored at `1e-3`. `compose` is its differentiable
  inverse.

#### 5.3.6 Robustness acceptance, not accuracy

12 perturbed restarts: rotation `U(5°, 30°)` about a random axis and `U(−5, +5)` mm per translation component,
each re-refined `0.3 rigid (150) → 0.3 affine (150) → 0.15 affine (150)`, counted converged at
`corner_mean_mm < 0.5` on the standardised **7 mm** lever arm (`evaluate.transform_diff(..., extent_mm=7.0)`).
Successful subjects score 8–12/12.

Say what this measures: **basin width, not correctness.** As §5.2.6 recorded, I58 and I61 are 12/12 and both
are wrong, while I46 and I55 — the two subjects with quantitative support — are 9/12 each. Restart consistency
belongs in the report as a robustness statistic and must never be presented as validation.
